REM (0.15 for Just-Bird, 0.2 for Birds-With-Labels; add --conf to change it) and merge.
echo Filtering raw detections at the model's default confidence and merging for confusion matrix...
python src\evaluation\filter_and_merge_detections.py ^
    --raw-detections "%OUTPUT_PATH%" ^
    --output-path "%OUTPUT_PATH%" ^
    --output-format all ^
    %MERGE_FLAGS%
if errorlevel 1 goto :fail


REM REM Step 4: Run confusion matrix analysis.
echo Running confusion matrix analysis...
python src\evaluation\confusion_matrix_analysis.py ^
    --detections "%OUTPUT_PATH%" ^
    --labels "%LABELS_CSV%" ^
    --output-path "%OUTPUT_PATH%\confusion_matrix_analysis" ^
    --iou-threshold 0.25 ^
    %SINGLE_CLS_FLAG%
if errorlevel 1 goto :fail


REM Step 5: Examine results in results\ directory
echo.
echo All tasks completed!
echo Results can now be examined in the %OUTPUT_PATH% directory.
exit /b 0

:fail
echo.
echo Pipeline failed. See the error above.
exit /b 1

docs.title: Ground-Truth Labels
docs.text:
Evaluation expects ground truth as a comma-separated CSV with a fixed header row. The layout matches the annotations.csv files of the Zenodo datasets listed in Available Models and Respective Datasets.

f_beta_score_analysis.py and confusion_matrix_analysis.py read this format with pandas.read_csv and require the exact column names below.

docs.title: Header (required, exact spelling)
docs.text: Filename,Start Time (s),End Time (s),Low Freq (Hz),High Freq (Hz),Species eBird Code

docs.title: Column Reference
docs.text:
Column Type Required? Description Filename string Yes Base recording name as stored on disk (e.g. SNE_001_17.wav). Used to match detections. See Filename matching. Start Time (s) float Yes Interval start in seconds from the beginning of that file. End Time (s) float Yes Interval end in seconds (must be ≥ start). Low Freq (Hz) number Yes Lower frequency bound of the annotation box in Hz. High Freq (Hz) number Yes Upper frequency bound in Hz. Species eBird Code string Yes Cornell/Clements eBird species code (e.g. herthr, amerob, cangoo).

There is no confidence column in ground truth. Inference CSV may add a seventh Confidence column. See Detection Output Formats for that format.

docs.title: Example Rows
docs.text:
From the Western-US test set:

Filename,Start Time (s),End Time (s),Low Freq (Hz),High Freq (Hz),Species eBird Code
SNE_001_17.wav,3.8,5.9,3219,4804,herthr
SNE_001_17.wav,0.0,7.6,2666,5405,herthr
SNE_001_17.wav,0.0,7.7,1297,4564,amerob

From the Northeastern-US test set:

Filename,Start Time (s),End Time (s),Low Freq (Hz),High Freq (Hz),Species eBird Code
SSW_001_0.wav,47.4,51.3,0,2647,cangoo
SSW_001_2.wav,0.0,0.6,0,4509,cangoo

Labels of unknown species

Annotators write ???? for a call whose species they could not name. The evaluation reads ???? as unknown, the code BirdBox uses for this class, and counts it as a class like any other. Birds-With-Labels has an unknown class too, so its unknown boxes can match these labels. With --single-cls, unknown labels count as bird like every other label.

Evaluating Just-Bird

Just-Bird names every box bird, while the labels name species. Pass --single-cls to f_beta_score_analysis.py and confusion_matrix_analysis.py. Every label and every detection then counts as bird.

docs.title: Filename matching
docs.text:
Matching pairs detections to labels per recording, using only the filename stem, which is the name without path and extension:

Label file Detection file Matched key SNE_001_17.wav SNE_001_17.flac SNE_001_17 SSW_001_0.wav SSW_001_0.wav SSW_001_0

Filename matching rules

  • The stem in Filename must agree between labels and detections. Case matters.
  • Different extensions between label CSV and detection export are fine.
  • Paths on disk do not matter. Only the Filename value counts, so two recordings with the same name in different folders are treated as one.

docs.title: Creating your own labels
docs.text:
1. Copy the header line exactly (including spaces and parentheses).
  2. Give times in seconds from the start of the recording and frequencies in Hz. Draw each box tight around the call in time and frequency. The evaluation matches labels and detections by the overlap of their boxes in both (IoU). The model sees 50 to 15,000 Hz, so a box that reaches far outside this range cannot overlap a detection well.
  3. Put the same Filename values you expect in detection outputs (typically the audio basename).
  4. Use eBird codes that exist in the Birds-With-Labels species mapping, or unknown for calls of unknown species (???? is read as unknown). No detection carries a code outside the mapping, so labels with such a code always count as missed. For Just-Bird any code works, since --single-cls maps them all to bird.

Labels from Raven or other tools work once they are converted to this six-column layout. A Raven selection table has no Filename column and names its time columns Begin Time (s) and End Time (s). Add the column, rename the others, and write the species code in Species eBird Code.

For CLI usage and invocation examples for each tool that reads this file, see f-beta-score-analysis and confusion-matrix-analysis.

docs.title: Audio and Model Inputs
docs.text: BirdBox reads field recordings and a trained YOLO weights file, then maps neural-network class IDs to species using a named mapping in src/config.py. This page documents the accepted formats for the --audio, --model, and --species-mapping inputs. For CLI flags, defaults, and invocation examples see the detect-birds reference.

docs.title: Audio inputs
docs.text: --audio may be a single file or a directory. Directories are searched recursively for supported files.

docs.title: Supported extensions
docs.text:
Extension Recommended? Notes .wav Yes Lossless. Fully supported. .flac Yes Lossless. Fully supported. .ogg Use with care Lossy. May reduce recall on faint or high-frequency calls. .mp3 Use with care Lossy. Same caveat as OGG.

Case is ignored (.WAV and .wav are both found).

docs.title: Processing behavior
docs.text:
• Mono conversion: Stereo recordings are averaged to mono before the spectrogram is computed.
  • Sample rate: Audio at a rate other than 32 kHz is resampled to 32 kHz.
  • Arbitrary length: Recordings of any length are processed in 3 s windows that overlap by half (see Merging the Windows).
  • Batch mode: Point --audio at a folder to process every supported file under it in one run. Batch mode starts at two recordings. A folder with one recording gives the same outputs as that file alone (see Detection Output Formats). Outputs and evaluation identify recordings by file name only, so give each recording a unique name across subfolders.

Lossy audio formats

MP3 and OGG are supported via soundfile, but compression can hide faint calls. In a study of avian recordings, MP3 compression reduced the detections of human listeners and automated recognisers [22]. If detections look weak on a compressed file, run the original WAV or FLAC recording before tuning thresholds. Converting an MP3 to WAV does not bring back what the compression removed. If only a compressed copy exists, a bitrate of 256 kbps or more keeps the losses small.

docs.title: Model files
docs.text:
--model must point to a YOLO-compatible weights file loaded by Ultralytics. BirdBox supports three formats:

Format Typical use Runtime .pt PyTorch checkpoint. The reference that the other formats are compared against. PyTorch (CUDA or CPU) .onnx Cross-platform deployment. Quantized variants available. ONNX Runtime (GPU or CPU) .tflite Edge devices and mobile targets. LiteRT / ai-edge-litert (CPU)

The pretrained models on TUC-Cloud come as .pt in fp32 and as .onnx and .tflite in fp16 and int8 (see Model Download). Custom models can be trained with BirdBox-Train.

Each format needs an environment with its runtime. Install it before you switch formats.

Environment must match the model format

An environment runs .pt models and the format it was installed for. Loading a .onnx or .tflite model without its runtime stops with an error that names the install command. Run python install.py --model-format <FORMAT> in a separate environment for each format. See Install Parameters for the full format-to-runtime table.

Format parity

Detection quality of the .onnx and .tflite formats is validated by running inference on the same audio and comparing results against the .pt baseline. See Just-Bird format parity and Birds-With-Labels format parity for the current scores.

docs.title: Species Mapping
docs.text:
The --species-mapping name must match the label space the model was trained on. It is not inferred from the weights filename. You pass it explicitly. For specific mappings see SPECIES_MAPPING in src/config.py.

Allowed values for the species-mapping parameter:

Value Classes Just-Bird One bird class for calls of any species Birds-With-Labels 632 species, an unknown class for calls of unknown species, and a bird class (see Birds-With-Labels)

Each key resolves to id_to_ebird, ebird_to_name, and display colors in src/config.py. The mapping name is stored in detection JSON as model_config.species_mapping.

Mapping must match the model

If --species-mapping does not match the class list the model was trained with, outputs carry wrong eBird codes with no error. Always pair model file and mapping from the same release (e.g. Birds-With-Labels_fp32.pt with Birds-With-Labels).

docs.title: References
docs.text: [22] MacPhail, A. G., Yip, D. A., Knight, E. C., Hedley, R., Knaggs, M., Shonfield, J., Upham-Mills, E., & Bayne, E. M. (2024). "Audio data compression affects acoustic indices and reduces detections of birds by human listening and automated recognisers." Bioacoustics, 33(1):74–90.

docs.title: File Flows
docs.text: BirdBox moves data through a small set of file types. Audio and models go in, detections and evaluation results come out. This section describes these files for pipeline scripts, external tools, and anyone wiring BirdBox into a larger workflow.

docs.title: File Flow for Detection Only
docs.text:
For field use or exporting annotations. No ground-truth CSV and no evaluation scripts. You run inference once at a chosen --conf. detect_birds.py merges the boxes of the overlapping windows itself (see Merging the Windows).

flowchart TB
  subgraph inputs ["Inputs"]
    audio[Audio WAV/FLAC/OGG/MP3]
    model[YOLO model .pt / .onnx / .tflite]
    mapping[species mapping]
  end

  subgraph detection ["Detection"]
    detect[detect_birds.py]
  end

  subgraph outputs ["Outputs"]
    outJSON[with_algorithm_metadata.json]
    outCSV[simplified.csv]
    outXC[xeno-canto-annota.json]
    outRaven[raven_selection_table.txt]
  end

  audio --> detect
  model --> detect
  mapping --> detect
  detect --> outJSON
  detect --> outCSV
  detect --> outXC
  detect --> outRaven

Use --output-format all to write every format in one run, or pick a single format. Details are on Detection Output Formats in this section.

docs.title: File Flow for Detection and Evaluation
docs.text:
For benchmarking on a labeled test set. Run detection once with --no-merge at a very low confidence, such as --conf 0.001. Find the best threshold against annotations.csv. Then filter and merge at a threshold and score the errors.

flowchart TB
  subgraph inputs ["Inputs"]
    audio[Audio WAV/FLAC/OGG/MP3]
    model[YOLO model .pt / .onnx / .tflite]
    mapping[species mapping]
    labels[annotations.csv]
  end

  subgraph detection ["Detection"]
    detect[detect_birds.py --no-merge]
    rawJSON[raw_detections.json]
  end

  subgraph tuning ["Fβ Score"]
    fbeta[f_beta_score_analysis.py]
    threshold[optimal --conf]
  end

  subgraph merge ["Filter and Merge"]
    filter[filter_and_merge_detections.py]
    outCSV[simplified.csv]
  end

  subgraph metrics ["Confusion Matrix"]
    cm[confusion_matrix_analysis.py]
  end

  audio --> detect
  model --> detect
  mapping --> detect
  detect --> rawJSON
  rawJSON --> fbeta
  labels --> fbeta
  fbeta --> threshold
  rawJSON --> filter
  threshold --> filter
  filter --> outCSV
  outCSV --> cm
  labels --> cm

The best threshold is in optimal_thresholds.csv of the F-beta step (see Reading the Optimal Thresholds File). Pass it to filter_and_merge_detections.py as --conf. Without --conf, filter and merge uses the model's default threshold, 0.15 for Just-Bird and 0.21 for Birds-With-Labels.

run_pipeline.sh at the repository root runs these four steps. It filters at the model's default threshold. Add --conf to its filter step to use the best threshold instead.

Just-Bird has one bird class, while the labels name species. Pass --single-cls to both evaluation scripts so that every label counts as bird. In run_pipeline.sh, USE_SINGLE_CLS=true sets it. This is the script's default. Set USE_SINGLE_CLS=false for Birds-With-Labels.

Step-by-step CLI usage for each script is under CLI Reference in the site navigation.

docs.title: Detection Output Formats
docs.text:
BirdBox can write inference results in four interchange formats. The same choices apply to detect_birds and filter_and_merge_detections. Both accept --output-format as a space-separated list or all.

Both commands take --output-path as an output directory. Each format writes a fixed, descriptive filename inside that directory.

detect_birds.py also writes args.yaml in that directory. It stores every CLI argument for the run so later inference folders can be compared. The evaluation scripts write their own args.yaml inside their result folders (for example results/f_beta_score_analysis/ and results/confusion_matrix_analysis/). filter_and_merge_detections.py writes no args.yaml. Its settings are in the filtering_config block of its JSON.

docs.title: Available Formats
docs.text: Value File(s) written Primary use json-with-algorithm-metadata with_algorithm_metadata.json (merged) or raw_detections.json (--no-merge) F-beta threshold sweeps via detect_birds --no-merge. Re-threshold without re-inference via filter_and_merge_detections. Archival output with full model_config. The evaluation pipeline reads raw_detections.json only. simplified-csv simplified.csv Confusion matrix analysis. The six columns of the ground-truth CSV, plus Confidence from detect_birds.py. xeno-canto-annota-json xeno-canto-annota.json Annota-JSON export for Xeno-Canto submission prep raven-selection-table raven_selection_table.txt (one recording) or raven/<Filename>.txt (batch mode) Raven manual review all All of the above One-shot export of every format

docs.title: Single recording and batch mode
docs.text:
Batch mode means a run over two or more recordings. A single file, or a folder with only one recording, gives single-recording output:

One recording Batch mode JSON top level audio_file audio_files and file_count filename, file_path in each detection No Yes Raven tables raven_selection_table.txt raven/<Filename>.txt per recording

filter_and_merge_detections.py keeps the form of the raw JSON it reads. It adds filename to every merged detection, also for one recording.

docs.title: 1. json-with-algorithm-metadata
docs.text:
Filename: with_algorithm_metadata.json or raw_detections.json depending on --no-merge parameter.

Holds the detections with all their fields and the settings of the run in model_config.

docs.title: Top-level structure
docs.text:
A Birds-With-Labels run with the default settings writes:

{
  "audio_file": "/path/to/recording.wav",
  "model_config": {
    "model": "models/Birds-With-Labels_fp32.pt",
    "confidence_threshold": 0.21,
    "nms_iou_threshold": 0.7,
    "song_gap_threshold": 0.1,
    "species_mapping": "Birds-With-Labels",
    "merge_method": "fusion",
    "floor_window_seconds": 60.0,
    "phrase_gap": 0.05,
    "bird_class_id": 633,
    "label_conf": 0.25
  },
  "detection_count": 130,
  "detections": [ /* see field tables below */ ]
}
model_config key Meaning model Path of the model file confidence_threshold --conf of the run nms_iou_threshold --nms-iou of the run song_gap_threshold --song-gap. Used by --merge reconstruct only. species_mapping --species-mapping of the run merge_method fusion or reconstruct (see Merging the Windows) floor_window_seconds Noise-floor window of the spectrograms, 60.0 s phrase_gap --phrase-gap. Written with fusion only. freq_iou_threshold Just-Bird only. --freq-iou, used by --merge reconstruct. bird_class_id, label_conf Birds-With-Labels only. Index of the bird class and --label-conf (see Species Names).

In batch mode, audio_file is replaced by "audio_files": [...] and "file_count": N. After filter_and_merge_detections, model_config stays as in the raw file and a filtering_config block holds the settings of the filter step:

{
  "filtering_config": {
    "confidence_threshold": 0.21,
    "song_gap_threshold": 0.1,
    "merge_method": "fusion",
    "freq_iou_threshold": null,
    "phrase_gap": 0.05,
    "label_conf": 0.25
  },
  "detection_count": 260,
  "original_detection_count": 14324,
  "detections": [ /* merged detections */ ]
}

docs.title: Raw detection objects
docs.text:
Produced by inference when --no-merge is set. Each object is one box of one 3 s window:

Field Type Description species string eBird code from species mapping species_id int YOLO class index confidence float Box confidence (0–1) time_start float Start time in seconds (file timeline) time_end float End time in seconds freq_low_hz number Low frequency bound (Hz) freq_high_hz number High frequency bound (Hz) clip_start float Start of the 3 s window (s) clip_end float End of that window (s) filename string Batch mode only. Basename of the source audio. file_path string Batch mode only. Full path to the source audio.

docs.title: Merged detection objects
docs.text:
Without --no-merge, the boxes of the overlapping windows are merged (see Merging the Windows). Each object is one merged box:

Field Type Description species string eBird code species_id int Class index time_start, time_end float Time bounds of the merged box (s) freq_low_hz, freq_high_hz number Frequency bounds of the merged box (Hz) avg_confidence float Mean confidence of the joined boxes, weighted by their detections_merged. A box that was not joined keeps its own confidence. max_confidence float Highest confidence among the joined boxes detections_merged int Number of window boxes behind the merged box filename string Batch mode, and always after filter_and_merge_detections.py. Basename of the source audio. file_path string Batch mode with detect_birds.py only. Full path to the source audio.

Window fusion averages overlapping boxes weighted by confidence, so its bounds are fractional. The phrase join and the song merge take the outer bounds of the joined boxes.

Birds-With-Labels boxes carry three more fields, raw and merged (see Species Names). Their species is bird when no species reaches the label threshold, and their confidence is the bird score. The species value can also be unknown, the class for calls of unknown species. Both names carry over to every other format. Annotation files and other tools may write unknown as ????. The evaluation tools read ???? as unknown.

Field Type Description species_confidence float Score of the top species alternatives list The top three species, best first, each with species, species_id and confidence bird_id int Class index of bird (633)

Raw vs merged in evaluation

f_beta_score_analysis.py reads raw JSON and re-applies filter-then-merge per confidence threshold. confusion_matrix_analysis.py expects merged intervals in simplified CSV, not this JSON.

docs.title: 2. simplified-csv
docs.text:
Filename: simplified.csv

Flat table with the six columns of the ground-truth annotations.csv. detect_birds.py adds a seventh Confidence column. filter_and_merge_detections.py writes the six columns only.

Filename,Start Time (s),End Time (s),Low Freq (Hz),High Freq (Hz),Species eBird Code[,Confidence]

docs.title: Column reference
docs.text: Column Description Filename Basename of the audio file (or per-detection filename in batch mode) Start Time (s) time_start, rounded to one decimal place End Time (s) time_end, one decimal place Low Freq (Hz) freq_low_hz, rounded to whole Hz High Freq (Hz) freq_high_hz, whole Hz Species eBird Code species Confidence detect_birds.py only. avg_confidence for merged boxes, confidence for raw boxes with --no-merge. Three decimals.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Filename,Start Time (s),End Time (s),Low Freq (Hz),High Freq (Hz),Species eBird Code,Confidence
SNE_001_17.wav,12.5,14.2,2151,5820,amerob,0.470
SNE_001_17.wav,25.3,27.8,1890,4560,herthr,0.612

The merged CSV is the usual input to confusion_matrix_analysis.py via --detections. It reads the six columns and ignores Confidence.

docs.title: 3. xeno-canto-annota-json
docs.text:
Filename: xeno-canto-annota.json

Exports a lean Annota-JSON payload for Xeno-Canto. BirdBox uses Cornell/Clements eBird codes internally. Xeno-Canto expects AviList scientific names in this format, see Taxonomy conversion.

The set-level envelope contains provenance fields and fixed BirdBox identifiers. Fields like set_uri, set_creator_id, set_owner, set_license, funding, and project_uri are left empty. Export-only XC fields (original_set_metadata, annotation_xc_id, etc.) are stripped before write.

docs.title: Per-annotation fields
docs.text:
Each detection becomes one object in annotations:

Field Source Description annotation_source_id generated birdbox-000001, … sound_file filename / file_path / audio_path Recording basename xc_nr parsed or "" XC number if filename contains XC123456 pattern annotator "BirdBox" Fixed annotator_xc_id "" User XC id (not set) frequency_low freq_low_hz Hz, three decimals frequency_high freq_high_hz Hz, three decimals start_time time_start Seconds, three decimals end_time time_end Seconds, three decimals scientific_name mapped AviList scientific name, or Aves for bird and unknown (see below) sound_type "call" Fixed default date_identified today's ISO date Date of export annotation_remarks built string Includes eBird code and confidence

Confidence in remarks uses avg_confidence when present, else confidence.

docs.title: Example (truncated)
docs.text:
{
  "set_source": "BirdBox detection results",
  "set_name": "BirdBox detection results",
  "annotation_software_name_and_version": "BirdBox",
  "scope": [{ "taxon_coverage": "Turdus migratorius, Catharus guttatus", "completeness": "part" }],
  "annotations": [
    {
      "annotation_source_id": "birdbox-000001",
      "sound_file": "recording.wav",
      "xc_nr": "",
      "scientific_name": "Turdus migratorius",
      "frequency_low": 2151.0,
      "frequency_high": 5820.0,
      "start_time": 12.5,
      "end_time": 14.2,
      "sound_type": "call",
      "annotation_remarks": "Detected by BirdBox; eBird code: amerob; confidence: 0.470"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Taxonomy conversion (eBird → AviList)
docs.text:
BirdBox labels use eBird/Clements codes. Annota-JSON expects AviList scientific names. BirdBox bridges this with:

  1. taxonomies/Cornell-to-AviList-mapping.json maps each lowercase eBird code to scientific_name and english_name.
  2. Order of lookups in build_xeno_canto_json:
  3. Aves for boxes without a species (bird and unknown)
  4. AviList mapping entry
  5. detection scientific_name if already set
  6. ebird_to_name from the active species mapping (scientific part before _)
  7. raw eBird code string

18 Birds-With-Labels codes have no AviList entry and take the scientific name from the species mapping. Split/merge caveats and how the mapping file is generated are documented in taxonomies/README.md in the repository.

Filter-and-merge export reads model_config.species_mapping from the input JSON when present.

docs.title: 4. raven-selection-table
docs.text:
Filename: raven_selection_table.txt (tab-separated, Raven Selection Table layout)

Species appear in the Annotation column as eBird codes (not common names). The table has no confidence column.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text: Column Value Selection 1-based index, sorted by time_start per file View Spectrogram 1 Channel 1 Begin Time (S) time_start (three decimals) End Time (S) time_end (three decimals) Low Freq (Hz) freq_low_hz, whole Hz High Freq (Hz) freq_high_hz, whole Hz Annotation species (eBird code)

docs.title: Single file vs batch
docs.text:
Input mode Output path behavior One recording (a file, or a folder with one recording) {output-path}/raven_selection_table.txt Batch mode (two or more recordings) {output-path}/raven/{Filename}.txt per recording

Example: --output-path results/run with several recordings results in results/run/raven/SNE_001_17.wav.txt, etc. Two recordings with the same name in different subfolders would write to the same table, so give each recording a unique name.

Filter-and-merge follows the same rule: a raw JSON from one recording gives one raven_selection_table.txt, a multi-file raw JSON gives raven/{Filename}.txt per recording. A Raven table has no filename column, so one table per recording keeps selections from other files off the spectrogram.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Selection   View    Channel Begin Time (S)  End Time (S)    Low Freq (Hz)   High Freq (Hz)  Annotation
1   Spectrogram 1   1   12.512  14.236  2151    5820    amerob
2   Spectrogram 1   1   25.304  27.817  1890    4560    herthr

docs.title: Adding Models to the Demo
docs.text:
The model menu lists the models in docs/models/manifest.json. The first one is the default. The instant sliders need the graph's per-window boxes (raw_all) and a JavaScript port of its merge: docs/javascripts/demo/fusion.js for window fusion (fusion, the export's default for both models) and docs/javascripts/demo/songs.js for song reconstruction (reconstruct, for a model exported with --merge reconstruct). The Just-Bird frequency gate (--merge reconstruct with Just-Bird) has no port. The demo skips such entries.

  1. Export the model.

    Linux / macOSWindows (PowerShell)Windows (CMD) 
    python src/inference/onnx_export.py \
    --output-path docs/models/Just-Bird_fp16.onnx \
    --precision fp16

    python src/inference/onnx_export.py `
    --output-path docs/models/Just-Bird_fp16.onnx `
    --precision fp16

    python src/inference/onnx_export.py ^
    --output-path docs/models/Just-Bird_fp16.onnx ^
    --precision fp16

    For another model, add --pt-model, for example --pt-model models/Birds-With-Labels_fp32.pt --output-path docs/models/Birds-With-Labels_fp16.onnx.

    --precision fp16 stores the network weights in fp16, which halves the file (20 MB instead of 38 MB for Just-Bird, 51 MB instead of about 100 MB for Birds-With-Labels). Feature extraction and merging stay in fp32. On 13 test recordings (tests/onnx_graph_parity.py), the fp16 graphs reproduced the boxes of detect_birds.py with the .pt model: 99.8% for Just-Bird (mean IoU 0.995) and 99.6% for Birds-With-Labels, with the same species (mean IoU 0.997). The export prints the merge it baked in (Merge (baked in), set with --merge) and the suggested defaults (Default conf and Default song_gap, set with --conf and --song-gap). It also stores them in the ONNX metadata. With window fusion, Default song_gap is the phrase gap.

  2. Place the .onnx file under docs/models/ if the export path was elsewhere.

  3. Add an entry to docs/models/manifest.json, first in the list if the demo should start with it.

    {
  "models": [
    {
      "file": "Just-Bird_fp16.onnx",
      "label": "Just-Bird_fp16.onnx (recommended)",
      "merge_method": "fusion",
      "conf": 0.15,
      "phrase_gap": 0.05,
      "species_mapping": "Just-Bird",
      "names": { "0": "bird" }
    },
    {
      "file": "Birds-With-Labels_fp16.onnx",
      "label": "Birds-With-Labels_fp16.onnx",
      "merge_method": "fusion",
      "conf": 0.21,
      "phrase_gap": 0.05,
      "species_mapping": "Birds-With-Labels",
      "bird_class_id": 633,
      "label_conf": 0.25,
      "names": { "0": "unknown", "1": "amabaw1", "…": "…", "633": "bird" },
      "common_names": { "0": "Unknown", "1": "Amazonian Barred-Woodcreeper", "…": "…", "633": "Bird (species unsure)" }
    }
  ]
}
    Field Meaning file The ONNX file, relative to docs/models/ label Name in the model menu merge_method fusion or reconstruct, as printed by the export. Other entries are skipped. conf Where the confidence slider starts: usually the printed Default conf (0.15 for Just-Bird, 0.21 for Birds-With-Labels, 0.2 for other models). phrase_gap fusion only: where the phrase gap slider starts, the printed Default song_gap, which is the phrase gap here (0.05 for both models) song_gap reconstruct only: where the song gap slider starts, the printed Default song_gap (0.1) species_mapping Written to model_config of the exported JSON bird_class_id Species models with a bird class only: the index of that class, the last one (633 for Birds-With-Labels). It turns on species naming. The merge then ignores species, and each merged box is named after the best species inside it. label_conf Species models with a bird class only: the score the best species needs to name a box. Below it, the box is named bird. 0.25 if left out. names eBird codes by class index, for the table and the exports (ONNX Runtime Web does not expose ONNX metadata) common_names Optional: common names by class index, shown in the table instead of the codes

    For a species model, names and common_names come from id_to_ebird and ebird_to_name of its mapping in src/config.py. With more than one class, the table gets a species column.

  4. Check that the demo's merge still matches the graph. The tests need Node.js 22, the version the CI uses.

    cd tests/js && npm install
node demo_merge_parity.mjs ../../docs/models/Just-Bird_fp16.onnx

    The script compares fusion.js or songs.js, whichever the manifest entry's merge_method names, with the graph's own detections for 48 slider settings (32 for song reconstruction) on tests/test.wav and fails on any difference. The network runs once. Each setting then runs only the graph's merge (mergeGraph in onnx-graph.js), so the check takes one to three minutes. Run it after exporting a new model or changing a merge in src/inference/onnx_export.py.

    The other demo tests in tests/js check the chunked and streamed runs, the boxes while recording and which boxes are dashed. They run in parallel processes, each on one ONNX Runtime thread like the demo, so the rows are the browser's:

    • npm test: every test on the manifest's first model, the demo's default. On the other models it runs the tests of their merge and one chunked run, because the models share all other code. About 4 minutes on a 20-core machine.
    • npm run test:all: every test on every model, for a new or newly exported model. About 10 minutes.
    • npm run test:serial: the tests one after another.

    The memory a machine has free decides how many processes run at once, at about 2 GB each, and --jobs=N sets that number. The demo tests workflow runs the tests on pull requests that change the demo, its models or these tests, and every test on every model when docs/models changes.

  5. Preview the demo. Install the docs tools with pip install -r requirements-docs.txt, run mkdocs serve from the repository root and pick the new model in the menu.

docs.title: Detection in the Demo
docs.text:
The Demo runs a self-contained BirdBox graph with ONNX Runtime Web in your browser. The graph computes the log-floor spectrogram, runs the YOLO detector on 3 s windows every 1.5 s and applies NMS, just like detect_birds.py with the same model. The model menu at the top picks the graph:

  • Just-Bird (docs/models/Just-Bird_fp16.onnx, the default): every box is a bird vocalization (bird), without species labels. For species, combine the boxes with BirdNET, see Species from BirdNET.
  • Birds-With-Labels (docs/models/Birds-With-Labels_fp16.onnx): the Birds-With-Labels model. It finds calls as Just-Bird does and names each box after its species, or bird when it is not sure. A bird box still shows its best guess, for example maybe Apapane · 0.18. On the five test datasets, that guess is right for about three in four bird boxes on a labelled call. On recordings from places outside the training data it is right less often, about one in three on Powdermill, a labelled set from Pennsylvania. Treat it as a hint. Hovering a box shows its top three species.

This page explains how the demo detects, while a file runs and while you record. Spectrogram explains what the viewer shows, Adding Models how to add a model to the menu.

docs.title: Boxes While It Runs
docs.text: New boxes appear after every 1.5 s of audio, and the part not analyzed yet is dimmed. Each window's noise floor comes from the 60 s before the window's end (rolling floor), so nothing depends on where a minute starts: the spectrogram is computed one window at a time and kept, and each window goes through the network as soon as its frames are there. The floor itself is computed in the page: each band's frames of the last 60 s are kept sorted, and from one window to the next only the 128 frames that leave and the 128 that arrive are merged in, so the network gets only the window's own frames (tests/js/demo_floor.mjs). The rows the graph returns, one per box of each window, are the same as in one run of the whole graph (tests/js/demo_chunk_parity.mjs).

docs.title: Pace
docs.text: Boxes appear at an even pace, although some windows take longer than others. The demo keeps a small buffer of finished windows, about 0.6 s of work, and shows them at the mean pace (docs/javascripts/demo/pacer.js, tests/js/demo_pacer.mjs). The progress line and, at the end, the summary show how many seconds of audio a second of detection covers ("9.5× real time").

docs.title: Dashed Boxes
docs.text:
Rows are final once they are there, but the next windows can still change the boxes near the end of the analyzed part: fuse them with theirs, hide them as nested, or join them into a phrase. Such boxes are dashed. That is the case when

  • it ends less than 1.5 s plus the gap (phrase gap or song gap) before the end of the analyzed part, or
  • it is linked to a dashed box: the same class, at most the gap apart and, with window fusion, overlapping in frequency.

The second rule covers a growing phrase. Its band widens as it takes in new calls, so it can still take in a box beside it that ended long before. Solid boxes do not change any more (docs/javascripts/demo/pending.js, tests/js/demo_dashed_boxes.mjs). Removed boxes are dashed as well, but in their own colour. The colour key in the demo's help shows both. With window fusion, the boxes no later window can reach are fused once and kept, so an update only fuses the newest rows, with the same boxes as fusing all rows anew (docs/javascripts/demo/fusion.js, tests/js/demo_fusion_parts.mjs).

docs.title: Stop and Continue
docs.text: Exports unlock when the whole recording is done. If you stop detection, Continue Detecting picks it up where it stopped, and the result is the same as an uninterrupted run. Run detection again starts over from the beginning of the recording. It starts with the 60 s of audio the next window's noise floor needs, not at the beginning of the recording, and computes their spectrogram 6 s at a time, to use less memory. If detection fails, the boxes found so far stay, and Continue Detecting goes on after them in a new worker. While it is stopped, you can export the boxes found so far, and a note under the export buttons says that the export does not cover the whole file. The file names of such exports end in _partial, and the JSON also states how far detection got (demo.partial, demo.analyzed_until_s, demo.audio_duration_s).

docs.title: Instant Sliders
docs.text:
The model runs once per recording, at the lowest confidence of the slider (0.05). The demo asks the graph for its per-window boxes (raw_all). When you move a slider, the demo drops the boxes below the new confidence and repeats the graph's merge in JavaScript. For both models that merge is window fusion: window ownership and weighted box fusion, removing nested boxes, joining calls into phrases. Birds-With-Labels merges its boxes without their species and then names each merged box from the boxes in it (Species Names).

This gives the same boxes as running the graph at the new confidence. The graph's NMS works inside each window, and there a box can only be suppressed by a box with a higher score. A box above the new confidence therefore survives NMS at 0.05 exactly when it survives NMS at the new confidence. The merge in JavaScript then gives the same boxes as the graph for any gap.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text: When you record, the spectrogram scrolls in from the right, and boxes appear a few seconds after a sound. A window's noise floor comes from the audio before its end, so each window is detected once, as soon as it is complete, and its rows are final. Only new audio becomes spectrogram frames, so a window takes a fraction of a second. Only the boxes the next windows may still change are dashed, as in a file. When you stop, only the last few windows are left, and the result is the same as loading the saved file (tests/js/rolling_floor_live.mjs). The page keeps the recording as a 32 kHz, 16-bit WAV, the format BirdBox reads, without the compression of a typical browser recording. The recording cannot be downloaded, and it is gone when you reload or leave the page. Nothing leaves your device.

docs.title: Review and Export
docs.text:
Boxes can be verified, moved, resized, removed and drawn. The exports use the BirdBox output formats: the JSON of --output-format json-with-algorithm-metadata, the simplified CSV and the Raven selection table, plus a CSV with every column of the table. For Birds-With-Labels, the JSON and the table CSV keep the top three species of each box, as species_confidence and alternatives (see Species Names).

Browser limits

  • The model is downloaded once (about 20 MB for Just-Bird, 51 MB for Birds-With-Labels) and then comes from the browser cache.
  • Audio must be at least 3 s long, one window.
  • Audio is decoded locally, resampled to 32 kHz mono and truncated to 10 minutes. The detection worker gets it 10 s at a time, so it holds a few seconds of audio rather than a copy of the file.
  • The browser's resampler is not librosa's, so files that are not recorded at 32 kHz can give slightly different boxes than the CLI.
  • ONNX Runtime runs single-threaded here: about 10 s for 2 minutes of audio on a laptop. Safari can be slower than Chromium or Firefox.
  • Use the CLI for long files and batch jobs.

docs.title: Spectrogram in the Demo
docs.text:
The viewer shows an STFT spectrogram by default. In its display settings, Log-floor switches to the log-floor mel spectrogram BirdBox detects on. The two are drawn for different readers. The STFT view is tuned so that calls stand out for people. The log-floor view is what the network is given, made as described in Spectrogram Generation. The figure shows both for ten seconds of the sample soundscape (40–50 s), with the boxes Just-Bird finds at the demo's defaults. Point at either view: the cross marks the same time and frequency in both.

Boxes The window shown below STFT viewthe default · linear, 0–15 kHz · Hann window of 1024 samples Log-floor viewwhat the model is given · mel, 50 Hz–15 kHz · flat-top window of 2048 samples
  • Background. The STFT view starts its colours 7 dB above each band's median, so ordinary noise is black. The model's picture starts 3 dB below the band's 20th percentile. It sees the noise as a purple texture and has to tell the calls from it. A box can therefore sit where the STFT view looks empty: on a faint sound that the STFT view draws black. Log-floor shows what the model saw there.
  • Frequency axis. Mel bands give low frequencies far more room. Half of the log-floor view lies below 2.7 kHz, while in the STFT view that range takes the bottom fifth.
  • Loudest colour. The STFT view turns white at the file's loudest 0.05 %, but never below 24 dB above the median (here at 24 dB). The model's picture always turns white at 45 dB above its floor.
  • Sharpness. The STFT's shorter window draws calls sharper in time and narrower in frequency. The model's flat-top window smears them, so its boxes can look loose on the STFT view.

docs.title: One Window
docs.text:
The network gets each 3 s window as a 256 × 256 image: the window's 252 frames stretched to 256 columns, the 256 mel bands as rows, and −3 to +45 dB above the window's noise floor in the 256 colours of inferno. This is the window from 43.5 to 46.5 s, marked in the figure above:

A window's pixels depend on its own noise floor, so the viewer shows each stretch of 1.5 s with the floor of the window that ends there, which are the pixels the model sees in the second half of that window. So for the second half of this window, 45 to 46.5 s, the log-floor view and the model's image hold the same values. The first half is drawn with the floor of the window before, which differs slightly. While recording, the floor is a running estimate over the last 60 s.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
Each picture cuts the audio into short frames and measures how loud the band at 4.0 kHz is in each. The grey areas show how often each loudness occurs, in dB above the band's median. 0 dB is the band's median in this recording, not a fixed sound level. Turning the recording up or down moves nothing in the chart. The tall hump is the background noise, which most frames hold. The thin tail to the right is the calls: rare, but up to 25–30 dB louder.

  • Model: the mel band, over the frames its noise floor is taken from. These are the 46.5 s up to the window's end, because the file starts at 0 s (see The Start of a File). The dashed line is their 20th percentile, the floor.
  • STFT view: one frequency bin of the STFT, over the whole file. Its hump is a little wider: a single bin of 31 Hz flickers more than a mel band, which adds up several bins over a longer window.

The bar under each row shows the range that picture spreads its colours over: levels left of the colours are black, levels right of them white. The model starts 3 dB below its floor, 6.6 dB below the median, so nearly all of the noise shows. The STFT view starts 7 dB above the median, so nearly all of the noise is black.

docs.title: The Start of a File
docs.text:
A window's noise floor comes from the 60 s up to its end. At the start of a file there is less: the first window's floor comes from its own 3 s, and only windows that end at 60 s or later get a full minute. With few frames the floor is less certain, and calls in a band lift its 20th percentile.

The figure shows the second minute of the sample, 60 to 120 s, as the model sees it. On top, as part of the long file, where every window's floor comes from the full minute before its end. In the middle, as the start of a recording that begins at 60 s, where the floor comes from the seconds since then. The bottom row shows how many dB the recording's picture is darker (blue) or brighter (orange) than the long file's, band by band. It is the difference of the two floors. Point at any of the three: the cross marks the same time and frequency in all of them.

The recording starts while the noise below 2 kHz is about 4 dB louder than in the minute before (the brighter low bands on the left of the top picture). Its floor knows only that louder noise, so for the first 6 s the bands below 2 kHz come out about 4 dB darker, and those from 2 to 10 kHz about 1 dB darker. The more of the minute the floor covers, the smaller the difference: about 3 dB below 2 kHz from 6 to 15 s, under 2 dB from 15 to 30 s, and almost none from 45 s on.

In the long fileeach window's floor from the minute before its end As the start of a recordingeach window's floor from the seconds since 60 s Differencethe recording's picture against the long file's

The two pictures are drawn as the log-floor view draws them, the loudest of every four frames per column.

On 64 starts cut from nine longer recordings, the floor 3 s into the file differed from the full minute's by 0.9 dB in the median band and by more than 3 dB in 18% of the bands. On average it was 0.4 dB higher, so the picture comes out slightly darker. With Just-Bird at the defaults, 13–16% of the boxes in the first 12 s changed (no box at IoU 0.5 in the other run), 9% from 12 to 30 s, 3.5% from 30 to 57 s, and none after 63 s. Against labels, the first 5 s of the Hawai'i validation recordings score 0.006–0.009 lower in F1 at IoU 0.5 than with a floor over each whole minute (BirdBox-Train repository, holdout_ssn/RESULTS.md). Just-Bird was trained with a floor over each whole minute, so it never saw such short floors.

A microphone that starts quiet pulls the floor down for up to 60 s, and the picture comes out brighter. With 0.5 s of near-silence at the start, 9% of the boxes from 6 to 12 s changed and 2% after 30 s. A fade-in of 0.3 s changes boxes mainly in the first seconds. Digital silence is left out of the floor.

The two views show this differently:

  • STFT view: its floor comes from the whole file, so the start looks like the rest of the file and shows none of this.
  • Log-floor view: it shows the model's pixels, the start included.
  • While recording: the log-floor view levels its first frames with a floor from the first 0.14 s, and later frames with one from a sample of the frames so far. It does not redraw them, so its first seconds can look brighter than what the model sees. After Stop, it shows the model's pixels.

docs.title: Frequency Axes
docs.text:
The figure splits both axes into three ranges, and the numbers give each range's share of the picture's height. Most of the bird song in the sample lies between 2 and 10 kHz (the coloured range), which takes about half of either picture: 53% of the STFT view and 45% of the model's rows. The mel scale moves room from the top to the bottom. Below 2 kHz gets 42% of the model's rows against 13% of the STFT view, and above 10 kHz gets 13% against 33%.

Why mel. The mel scale was built from listeners' judgements of pitch [32]. It became the frequency axis of speech recognition after mel-frequency cepstral coefficients beat the other representations compared for recognising spoken words [3]. In bioacoustic deep learning, mel spectrograms are common, but linear and logarithmic axes are used too, and evaluations have favoured each of the three. A review of the field calls the mel scale, an approximation of human hearing, an odd choice for animal sounds whose use likely owes a lot to convenience [33]. BirdNET's authors argue that the spectrogram should follow the vocal and auditory capabilities of birds rather than human speech. BirdNET uses a mel scale with 64 bands from 150 Hz to 15 kHz, with a break frequency of 1750 Hz instead of the 700 Hz of the common formula [13]. BirdBox uses the common formula (HTK, 700 Hz) and has not compared it with other frequency axes. With BirdNET's break frequency, 2 to 10 kHz would take 51% of BirdBox's rows instead of 45%.

The model's flat-top window separates frequencies about 59 Hz apart. Below 4.3 kHz the mel bands lie closer than that, so neighbouring rows mostly repeat each other, and that range takes 159 of the 256 rows. Above it the bands are wider than the window's resolution: about 100 Hz per row from 6 to 10 kHz, where many songbirds sing. A linear axis with 256 rows would have 59 Hz per row. In favour of mel, narrow low calls, such as those of owls and doves, get several rows each. On a roughly logarithmic axis, a harmonic call that is sung higher keeps its shape and only moves up, which suits a convolutional network [33].

docs.title: The Two Views Compared
docs.text:
STFT view Log-floor view and the model Window and hop Hann, 1024 samples (32 ms), every 10 ms Flat-top, 2048 samples (64 ms), every 11.7 ms Frequencies Linear, 0–15 kHz, 31 Hz per row 256 mel bands, 50 Hz–15 kHz Noise floor Each band's median over the whole file Each band's 20th percentile over the 60 s before each window's end, less at the start of a file Black at 7 dB above the median 3 dB below the floor White at The file's loudest 0.05 %, at least 24 dB above the median 45 dB above the floor Recorder gain Cancels out Cancels out While recording A running estimate of each band's median over the last 20 s A running estimate of the floor over the last 60 s

Brightness, contrast and the colour map in the display settings change how either view looks, never what the model gets. scripts/make_spectrogram_views.mjs makes the figures from the demo's own spectrogram code (docs/javascripts/demo/spec-worker.js, the viewer's colours at their defaults) and the Just-Bird graph at the demo's defaults. It also checks that the log-floor view holds the model's values for the window.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
[3] Davis, S. B., & Mermelstein, P. (1980). "Comparison of parametric representations for monosyllabic word recognition in continuously spoken sentences." IEEE Transactions on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing, 28(4):357–366.

[13] Kahl, S., Wood, C. M., Eibl, M., & Klinck, H. (2021). "BirdNET: A deep learning solution for avian diversity monitoring." Ecological Informatics, 61:101236.

[32] Stevens, S. S., Volkmann, J., & Newman, E. B. (1937). "A scale for the measurement of the psychological magnitude pitch." The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 8(3):185–190.

[33] Stowell, D. (2022). "Computational bioacoustics with deep learning: a review and roadmap." PeerJ, 10:e13152.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This chapter explains how BirdBox turns a recording into boxes, in Python and in the browser.

docs.title: Inference
docs.text:
BirdBox detects with YOLO on a sliding window: it computes a log-floor mel spectrogram, cuts it into 3 s windows every 1.5 s, runs the model on each window and merges the boxes of overlapping windows into one set of detections.

  • Algorithm Overview: the steps from the audio file to the detections, and how the boxes of overlapping windows are merged (window fusion and the song merge).
  • Spectrogram Generation: how the spectrogram and the model's 256 × 256 images are made, stage by stage.
  • Troubleshooting: what to try with no detections, too many false positives, boxes too long or too short, a silent recording in the demo, memory or runtime issues and mismatched file names.

docs.title: Demo
docs.text:
The Demo runs the same steps in the browser, as one ONNX graph that also computes the spectrogram.

  • Detection: the models in the menu, boxes while a file runs, the instant sliders, recording, review and export, and the browser's limits.
  • Spectrogram: the viewer's STFT view next to the log-floor view the model is given.
  • Adding Models: exporting a model to ONNX and adding it to the model menu.

docs.title: Algorithm Overview
docs.text:
This section describes the algorithmic ideas and the concepts utilized within BirdBox during inference.

For user-facing parameters see CLI Reference or API Reference. To compare different models, take a look at Models and Metrics. If you are interested in the file flow see File Flows.

docs.title: Inference Algorithm Concept
docs.text:
The key idea of the BirdBox inference is to use YOLO[26] from Ultralytics[12] with a sliding window approach. Both BirdBox models are YOLO11 object detectors: Just-Bird (YOLO11s, one bird class) and Birds-With-Labels (YOLO11l, 632 species, an unknown class for calls of unknown species, and a bird class). YOLO cannot run on continuous audio, so the recording is cut into short, overlapping images:

  1. Load the audio. It is mixed to mono and resampled to 32 kHz. Silence is added at the end so that the last 3 s window is complete; boxes in that silence are cut at the real end of the file.
  2. Compute a log-floor mel spectrogram with STFT[1]: log power minus each band's noise floor over the 60 s up to each clip's end, so a clip's boxes are final as soon as the audio reaches its end. It does not change with the recording level (details).
  3. Cut 3 s clips every 1.5 s (50% overlap) and render each as a 256×256 pixel image. BirdNET analyzes audio in 3 s segments as well [13].
  4. Run YOLO on the clips in batches. Boxes below the confidence threshold are dropped (default 0.15 for Just-Bird, 0.21 for Birds-With-Labels), and overlapping boxes within a clip are reduced by non-maximum suppression [11] (--nms-iou, default 0.7).
  5. Convert the boxes from pixels to seconds and Hz. The frequency axis follows the HTK mel scale from 50 Hz to 15 kHz, the inverse of how the training labels were drawn.
  6. Merge the boxes of overlapping windows into one set of detections per file, with window fusion, see below. Birds-With-Labels then names each box after its species, see Species Names.
  7. Write the detections in the selected output formats.

To examine the generation of the spectrograms in detail, see Spectrogram Generation. The various output data formats provided by BirdBox can be examined in Detection Output Formats.

docs.title: Merging the Windows
docs.text:
Consecutive windows overlap by half, so almost every call is seen by two windows. Any vocalization of 1.5 s or less lies completely inside at least one window; only longer vocalizations can be cut into parts. The two views of a call rarely give exactly the same box, and the merge decides what is kept. BirdBox has two merges. Both models use window fusion by default, and --merge reconstruct picks the song merge.

The figure shows both merges on six seconds of the demo sample. The song merge unions the two views of a call and joins calls less than 0.1 s apart, so the two calls at 9.5–10.1 s become one box. Window fusion keeps one box for each of them.

docs.title: Window Fusion
docs.text:
Window fusion keeps one box per call, or per phrase with a phrase gap. It works in four steps. The figure below shows each step on another six seconds of the demo sample. Solid boxes are what a step keeps, and dashed boxes what it removes or merges into others.

  1. Ownership. Each window owns its middle half (the thick lines at the top). The first window also owns the start of the file, the last one the end. A box is kept only from the window that owns its centre, which is the window that sees the call most centrally. The middle halves tile the file, so every call is kept once. The calls at 43.8 and 44.2 s were boxed by both windows, and only the boxes of the window that owns them stay. A call that only the other window found is lost: the faint call at 44.7 s and 2.5–4.5 kHz was boxed only by a window whose middle half ends at 44.25 s.
  2. Weighted box fusion. YOLO's non-maximum suppression within a window leaves boxes that overlap less than IoU 0.7. Of the boxes kept after step 1, those that overlap at 2D IoU ≥ 0.4 are averaged, weighted by confidence [30], and keep the strongest confidence. At 47.2–49.5 s two boxes of one window become one.
  3. Drop nested boxes. A box that lies at least 80% inside a larger box is removed, for example a syllable inside the box of its whole call. At 46.3–47.2 s the box of the first call goes, because it lies inside the longer box that starts with it. The step keeps the larger box even when it is the less confident one. Nested boxes are dropped before the join, so a removed box cannot change a joined box later.
  4. Join. Boxes in the same frequency band (frequency IoU ≥ 0.8) that overlap in time by at least 0.05 s are linked, for example a long call that two windows cut differently. Every group of linked boxes becomes one box, and this repeats on the joined boxes until nothing joins. With a phrase gap above 0, boxes closer than the gap are linked instead, so syllables become phrase boxes. Both models use 0.05 s by default, and --phrase-gap 0 keeps one box per call. In the figure the boxes from 46.3 s on become one phrase box, which continues to 62.4 s, and the boxes before 43 s become one.

Fusion was chosen in a design test with models trained on each dataset alone. On test sets labelled per call, it raised F1 at IoU 0.5 over the song merge, from 0.515 to 0.582 on Hawai'i and from 0.615 to 0.637 on Southern Sierra Nevada. F1 was counted over the boxes of all files together (micro F1). For the flags, see Merge Method.

docs.title: Phrase Gap
docs.text:
Some datasets box every syllable, others one box per phrase or song. The phrase gap sets how far apart boxes in one band may be and still be joined. Only this time rule changes with the gap, so the boxes change gradually as it grows. Both models default to 0.05 s, because they are run on recordings labelled in any of these ways.

Each point is the best F1 over all thresholds on full recordings, and the y-axes differ between the plots. The first two plots use the Just-Bird recipe trained without Southern Sierra Nevada. The third uses the released models on the 297 one-minute pieces of the Western US validation split. The models did not train on these minutes, but on other minutes of the same recordings.

On call labels the score falls steadily as the gap grows, while on phrase and song labels it barely moves. The 0.05 s default costs 0.005 on Hawai'i and adds at most 0.005 on the other two sets. The current Just-Bird model is well ahead of the October 2026 model on song labels at every gap, because it draws phrase boxes where its training labels did. For the values to pass, see Phrase Gap.

docs.title: Song Merge
docs.text:
The song merge (--merge reconstruct) joins detections of the same species whose gap is at most the song gap (--song-gap, default 0.1 s) into one song box that spans all of them. It suits labels that box whole songs. For Just-Bird, boxes are only joined if they also share the frequency band, so calls of different birds are not chained.

For details, see Song Gap Threshold.

docs.title: Species Names
docs.text:
Birds-With-Labels has a bird class next to its species, trained on every box whatever its species. The bird score finds the calls, as Just-Bird's single class does. The species scores then name them:

  1. Boxes from the bird score. The candidate boxes of a window whose bird score reaches the confidence threshold go through non-maximum suppression on the bird score, across species. So one call gets one box, never one box per species.
  2. Species from the boxes around it. Each kept box takes, per species, the highest score among those candidate boxes (before the suppression) that overlap it at IoU 0.5 or more.
  3. A name when the model is sure. A box is named after its top species when that score reaches 0.25 (--label-conf), and bird otherwise. The output keeps the top three species with their scores as alternatives.
  4. Merging without names. Window fusion runs on all boxes as one class, as for Just-Bird. Each merged box then takes, per species, the highest score among the window boxes from step 2 whose centre lies inside it, and is named the same way.

The confidence of a box is its bird score. species_confidence is the score of its top species. Bird Class and Names explains how the class was trained and how reliable the names are.

docs.title: Filter, Then Merge
docs.text: The confidence threshold is applied to the raw boxes of each window, before merging. The evaluation tools work the same way: detect_birds.py --no-merge writes the raw boxes once, and F-beta analysis or Filter and Merge Detections filter them at any threshold and merge them as detection would.

docs.title: Spectrogram Generation
docs.text:
BirdBox converts raw audio into log-floor mel spectrograms before running YOLO detection: log power in decibels minus each frequency band's noise floor. This page documents the complete preprocessing pipeline. Following these steps exactly lets you reproduce the same spectrogram representation used during both training and inference.

For the full implementation details, you can have a look at log_floor.py.

docs.title: Pipeline at a Glance
docs.text:
The pipeline runs in six sequential stages:

  1. Load the audio, mix it to mono and scale it (the factor cancels in stage 5)
  2. Resample to 32,000 Hz, pad the end and split the audio into one-minute segments
  3. Compute the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT)
  4. Apply a mel filterbank to compress frequency bins
  5. Convert to decibels and subtract each band's noise floor (log-floor)
  6. Extract fixed-length clips and render them as 256×256 pixel images

Stages 3 to 6 run once per segment, and segments only bound the memory: a clip's pixels do not depend on where a segment starts. Each step is described in detail below, including all parameter values.

docs.title: Stage 1: Audio Loading and Scaling
docs.text:
BirdBox reads audio using soundfile, with a librosa fallback for problematic files. Stereo recordings are mixed down to mono by averaging both channels.

The amplitude is then scaled to the integer range before any spectral processing:

audio = (audio * (2 ** 31)).astype("float32")

This maps the normalized float input, typically in [-1.0, 1.0], into the range of a 32-bit signed integer. The scaling is kept from the training pipeline. Log-floor itself does not depend on it: any constant factor cancels when the noise floor is subtracted.

docs.title: Stage 2: Resampling, End Padding and Segments
docs.text:
All audio is resampled to a fixed sample rate using librosa.resample. Files already at the target rate are passed through without modification.

The clips start every 1.5 s. If the file does not end on that grid, or is shorter than 3 s, silence is added at the end until the last clip is complete. Boxes that the model finds in this silence are cut at the real end of the file, and boxes that start after it are dropped.

The spectrogram is not computed for the whole file at once. To bound the memory, the audio is split into one-minute segments, and each clip is taken from the segment in which it starts. A segment's spectrogram reaches back to the start of its first clip's noise-floor window (up to 60 s before the segment) and 2 s past its end, so every clip of the segment and its floor window are complete. All segments use one frame grid for the whole file, so a clip's pixels are the same whichever segment computes them. Segments are independent, so for a single file --num-workers computes them in parallel (for several files it processes the files in parallel).

Parameter Value Target sample rate 32,000 Hz Segment length 60 s Audio before a segment its first clip's floor window, up to 60 s Audio after a segment 2 s End padding silence up to the end of the last 3 s clip

docs.title: Stage 3: Short-Time Fourier Transform
docs.text:
The STFT is computed using librosa.stft[23] with the following parameters. Note that the window length equals the FFT size to avoid zero-padding artifacts inside the analysis window.

Parameter Value Notes n_fft 2048 FFT size; sets frequency resolution win_length 2048 Equals n_fft; no zero-padding inside window hop_length 375 Frame step in samples (~11.72 ms per frame) window "flattop" Flat-top window for accurate amplitude representation center False No edge-padding; frames start at sample 0

The power spectrogram is derived from the complex STFT output:

stft = librosa.stft(audio, n_fft=2048, win_length=2048,
                    hop_length=375, window="flattop", center=False)
abs2_stft = np.abs(stft) ** 2

The ONNX graphs of the Demo and of onnx_export.py compute the same spectrum in two stages of matrix products (a 32 × 64 Cooley-Tukey transform), because matrix products run everywhere, also in browsers. On 14 test recordings, no pixel of the image was more than one of its 256 color steps away from a double-precision transform.

docs.title: Why flat-top?
docs.text: A flat-top window has a very flat passband in the frequency domain. This minimizes amplitude error for tonal signals, which is important for accurately representing bird vocalizations that may be near bin boundaries. This error between bins is known as scalloping loss [8], and flat-top windows are designed to keep it small [9].

docs.title: Stage 4: Mel Filterbank
docs.text:
The power spectrogram is mapped onto a mel-scale filterbank using librosa.feature.melspectrogram. BirdBox uses the HTK mel formula throughout, consistent with both training and inference.

Parameter Value Notes n_mels 256 Number of mel bands (output height) fmin 50 Hz Lowest frequency included fmax 15,000 Hz Highest frequency included htk True Uses the HTK formula, not the Slaney formula 
melspec = librosa.feature.melspectrogram(
    S=abs2_stft, sr=32000, n_fft=2048,
    n_mels=256, fmin=50, fmax=15000, htk=True
)

Frequency Range

The 50–15,000 Hz range covers the vast majority of bird vocalizations while discarding low-frequency rumble and ultrasonic content above the range of interest. The HTK formula spaces mel bands differently than the Slaney formula. Using the wrong formula at inference will produce mismatched filterbanks and degrade detection performance.

docs.title: Stage 5: Log-Floor Normalization
docs.text:
The mel power is converted to decibels, and each mel band's noise floor is subtracted: the 20th percentile of that band's levels over the 60 s up to the end of the clip (the rolling floor; fewer seconds at the start of a file). The image therefore shows how far each sound rises above the background of its own band. Values from 3 dB below to 45 dB above the floor fill the colour range (0 to 100 on the image scale); louder sounds take the brightest colour.

db = 10 * np.log10(np.maximum(melspec, 1e-10))     # frames of the file's frame grid
sound = melspec.sum(axis=0) > 0                    # leave out digital silence
# the frames that end by the clip's end and start at most 60 s before it
window = slice(first_frame_of_floor_window, last_frame_of_clip + 1)
floor = np.percentile(db[:, window][:, sound[window]], 20, axis=1, keepdims=True)
features = (db[:, clip_frames] - floor + 3.0) * (100.0 / 48.0)   # -3..45 dB above the floor -> 0..100
Parameter Value Role Floor percentile 20 The background level of each band over the floor window Floor window the 60 s up to the clip's end One floor per band and clip; no audio after the clip enters it Lowest colour 3 dB below the floor Quiet background stays dark but visible Brightest colour 45 dB above the floor Nearly no call reaches it (less than 0.15% of the pixels inside labelled calls) Digital silence left out of the floor The padding at the end of a file does not pull the floor down

What it gives. A recorder's gain adds the same number of decibels to every band and cancels when the floor is subtracted, so the same scene gives the same image whatever the recording level. A loud sound barely moves a 20th percentile, so the quiet tail after a loud call stays visible.

Why a rolling floor. Nothing after a clip changes its pixels, so a clip's boxes are final as soon as the audio reaches its end. A recording in progress gets the boxes of the saved file while it is still recording (see Recording in the demo), and the boxes of a clip do not depend on where a minute starts. Just-Bird was trained with a floor over each clip's whole 60 s segment. With the rolling floor it scores level on the validation and hold-out recordings, and slightly better on long files (results in the BirdBox-Train repository, holdout_ssn/RESULTS.md). Birds-With-Labels was trained on rolling-floor images.

Why not PCEN. Per-Channel Energy Normalization (PCEN) is the common alternative. It was introduced for keyword spotting [34]. On recordings of natural environments it brings the distribution of magnitudes close to a Gaussian and decorrelates the frequency bands [20], and for bird flight calls it reduced overfitting to the time of day [21]. With BirdBox's settings it kept about a quarter of the recording level in the image, so a model learned the level of its training recordings: with the Southern Sierra Nevada recordings played 12 dB louder, recall dropped from 0.53 to 0.38, and with the Hawai'i recordings 12 dB quieter it made many more faint false alarms. Its 1 s smoother also dimmed the quiet tail after a loud onset. Log-floor matched or beat PCEN on a site the models never saw, and its output does not change with the recording level (results in the BirdBox-Train repository, holdout_ssn/RESULTS.md).

docs.title: Frame Grid
docs.text:
Frame m of a file covers the samples from 375 m - 250 to 375 m - 250 + 2048, and clip c (starting at 1.5 c s) is frames 128 c to 128 c + 251. The offset of 250 samples is kept from the pipeline the training images were made with. It copied the first 0.5 s of the audio in front of it before the STFT and dropped the 42 frames that covered it, so the first kept frame started 250 samples before the file. The samples before the file start are therefore that copy (audio[15750:16000]), as in training.

Parameter Value left_pad_length 0.5 s (16,000 samples at 32 kHz) Pad frames dropped afterwards 42 (16,000 // 375)

docs.title: Stage 6: Clip Extraction and Image Rendering
Clip Parameters
docs.text:
Fixed-length clips are extracted from the log-floor output using a sliding window with 50% overlap. Each clip covers exactly 3 seconds of audio.

Parameter Value Clip length 3 s (252 frames) Clip hop 1.5 s (50% overlap) Output shape per clip 256 × 252 (mel bands × time frames)

The 252 frames start 375 samples apart, so their starts span 251 × 375 / 32,000 ≈ 2.94 s. With the 2048-sample window, the frames cover 251 × 375 + 2,048 = 96,173 samples, about 3.005 s. BirdBox calls this 3 s.

docs.title: Image Rendering
docs.text:
Each clip is rendered as a 256×256 pixel PNG using matplotlib, with all axes and labels stripped. The image is produced at exactly 100 DPI from a 2.56×2.56-inch figure.

fig = Figure(figsize=(2.56, 2.56), dpi=100)
ax = fig.add_subplot(111)
librosa.display.specshow(
    features, sr=32000, hop_length=375,
    ax=ax, cmap="inferno", vmin=0.0, vmax=100.0
)
ax.axis("off")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0, right=1, top=1, bottom=0)
Parameter Value Figure size 2.56 × 2.56 inches DPI 100 (yields 256×256 pixels) Colormap inferno vmin 0.0 vmax 100.0

Exact Parameters Required

The vmin and vmax values are baked into the model's training distribution. Using a different colormap or rescaling will shift pixel intensities relative to what the YOLO model was trained on, causing unpredictable detection results.

docs.title: Complete Pipeline Reference
docs.text:
The table below summarizes every numerical parameter across all stages for quick reference.

Stage Parameter Value Loading Amplitude scale × 2³¹ (cancels in log-floor) Resampling Target sample rate 32,000 Hz Segments Length 60 s, with the floor window before and 2 s after (memory only) Segments End padding silence up to the end of the last clip STFT n_fft 2048 STFT win_length 2048 STFT hop_length 375 STFT window "flattop" STFT center False Mel filterbank n_mels 256 Mel filterbank fmin 50 Hz Mel filterbank fmax 15,000 Hz Mel filterbank htk True Log-floor Floor 20th percentile of each band over the 60 s up to each clip's end (digital silence left out) Log-floor Range -3 to 45 dB above the floor → 0 to 100 Log-floor Frame grid frame m starts at sample 375 m - 250; before the file, audio[15750:16000] Clips Clip length 3 s / 252 frames Clips Clip hop 1.5 s (50% overlap) Image Size 256 × 256 px Image Colormap inferno Image vmin / vmax 0.0 / 100.0
