docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: This section provides information for typical mistakes one can make when interacting with BirdBox.

docs.title: No Detections
docs.text:
If BirdBox returns an empty results file, the most common cause is a model/mapping mismatch or a threshold that is set too high for exploratory work.

  • Verify that --model and --species-mapping belong together: Just-Bird for Just-Bird_fp32.pt, Birds-With-Labels for Birds-With-Labels_fp32.pt.
  • Lower the confidence threshold for exploratory runs. The defaults are 0.15 for Just-Bird and 0.21 for Birds-With-Labels. Try --conf 0.1, or --conf 0.001 to capture every raw hit.
  • Check audio format and quality. WAV and FLAC outperform lossy formats such as MP3 and OGG for faint or distant calls. In a study of avian recordings, MP3 compression reduced the detections of human listeners and automated recognisers [22].
  • Confirm that the audio file actually covers the time ranges recorded in your labels when running an evaluation.

Quick sanity check

Run BirdBox on a short clip you know contains a loud, clear call. If that also returns nothing, the issue is almost certainly the model/mapping pair, not the audio.

docs.title: Too Many False Positives
docs.text:
False positives usually indicate that the confidence threshold is too permissive or that overlapping detections are being merged incorrectly.

  • Increase --conf to raise the detection bar. Even a small step, for example from the default 0.15 to 0.25, can cut noise significantly.
  • Tune --nms-iou to control how aggressively duplicate bounding boxes within a window are suppressed. Lower values suppress more.
  • Run confusion_matrix_analysis.py and inspect the background row and column to distinguish species confusion from generic noise hits.

docs.title: Boxes Too Long or Too Short
docs.text:
Box length depends on the merge (see Merging the Windows) and should match how your labels are drawn.

Both models use window fusion by default:

  • The model boxes single syllables, but your labels box phrases or songs: raise --phrase-gap (default 0.05 s, try 0.1 to 0.5) so nearby syllables in the same band are joined.
  • The model joins calls that your labels keep apart: pass --phrase-gap 0 for one box per call.
  • With --merge reconstruct, unrelated calls end up in one long song box: reduce --song-gap (default 0.1 s). Raise it to join songs across longer pauses.

docs.title: Recording in the Demo Is Silent
docs.text: The Demo warns while recording when no sound arrives from the microphone for 1.5 s, and shows the input level under the timer. If the warning appears, check that the microphone is not muted, turned all the way down, or blocked for the browser in the system settings.

docs.title: Memory or Runtime Issues
docs.text:
Large audio collections can put pressure on RAM or stretch runtimes. Process smarter before scaling up hardware.

  • Reduce parallelism by lowering --num-workers for inference and F-beta analysis.
  • Process subsets of files and merge the resulting reports afterwards rather than running everything in one pass.
  • Prefer GPU-backed runs for large jobs when a compatible device is available.

Avoid redundant inference

Generate the raw detections JSON once using --no-merge. Re-running full inference just to experiment with confidence thresholds wastes significant time on large datasets.

docs.title: Filename Mismatch in Evaluation
docs.text:
Evaluation tools match audio files against labels using the normalized stem, which is the base filename with the extension stripped. If stems do not match, the file is silently skipped.

Audio file Label file Result recording_01.wav recording_01.flac Match siteA_recording_01.wav recording_01.flac No match

How to fix a mismatch

Inspect both the filename fields in your detection CSV or JSON and the filenames in your labels CSV. Unify the base names in one of the two sources, then re-run metrics.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [22] MacPhail, A. G., Yip, D. A., Knight, E. C., Hedley, R., Knaggs, M., Shonfield, J., Upham-Mills, E., & Bayne, E. M. (2024). "Audio data compression affects acoustic indices and reduces detections of birds by human listening and automated recognisers." Bioacoustics, 33(1):74–90.

docs.title: Bird Class and Names
docs.text: The Birds-With-Labels model has a class that is no species: bird. It finds the calls, and the species classes name them. This page explains why it is there, how it is trained, how a box gets its name and how far the names can be trusted.

docs.title: Why a Bird Class
docs.text:
A detector with one class per species finds a call only if it recognises the species. Two things work against it:

  • Every species learns from its own boxes alone. The training split has 559,368 call boxes. The median species has 134 of them, and 160 species have fewer than 50.
  • Unsure means several low scores. Where several species are possible, each of their classes gives the call a low score. A threshold low enough to find the call then draws one box per species.

Just-Bird has one class, so every box teaches it what a call looks like. The bird class brings the same signal into the species model:

A lower threshold helps the species classes only in part. At 0.05 the previous model covers as many of Just-Bird's boxes in 14 soundscapes from other places (77%) as the bird class does. But then 27% of its boxes lie where Just-Bird has none, against 7% for the bird class.

docs.title: How It Learns
docs.text:
Step 3 of the training recipe adds bird as the last class (id 633). Three things change in the training loss:

flowchart LR
  box["A call label,<br/>Ovenbird"]
  assign["Positions in the image<br/>that fit the box best,<br/>ranked by the bird score"]
  bird["Target for bird"]
  species["Target for Ovenbird"]
  shape["Target for the box"]
  teacher["Species teacher"]
  all["All species scores"]
  box --> assign
  assign --> bird
  assign --> species
  assign --> shape
  teacher -. distillation .-> all
  1. Every box trains two classes, bird and its species. Boxes of the class unknown train bird as well.
  2. The bird score decides which positions learn a box. YOLO assigns each label to the positions in the image that already predict it best, by class score and overlap (task-aligned assignment [4]). Here the class score is always that of bird. So the boxes follow the calls, not the species.
  3. Distillation goes on. The species teacher, which is the previous model, still teaches the species scores. It has no bird class, so bird learns from the labels alone.

The new class needs a start. With random weights it would need most of the ten epochs to react at all. It starts as the mean of the trained species classes instead, which already responds to what the calls of many species share.

docs.title: From Score to Name
docs.text:
For each 3 s window the model gives every box a bird score and 633 other scores:

  1. The bird score finds the box. Boxes above the confidence threshold (0.21) go through non-maximum suppression on that score, across all species. So one call gets one box.
  2. The boxes around it vote on the name. For each species, the highest score counts among the boxes that overlap it at IoU 0.5 or more.
  3. The top species names the box if its score is at least 0.25. Otherwise the box is named bird. The output keeps the three best species as alternatives.

Species Names describes how names survive the merge of overlapping windows.

Asking the neighbours in point 2 is better than reading the box's own species scores. On the song-labelled tests it adds 0.010 to 0.021 to macro F1. On the 14 soundscapes from other places, 39% of the boxes have a species score of at least 0.1, against 26%.

docs.title: How Reliable Are the Names
docs.text:
Every box of the test sets was compared with the labels. A box lies on a call when at least half of it is inside a label, or at least half of a label is inside it. Right and wrong are counted only for boxes on a call of a known species. Boxes off any label are left out, because the labels cannot say what they are. The boxes are those before merging:

Test set Boxes with a name Named boxes off any label Named boxes on a labelled call: right bird boxes on a labelled call: first guess right Five datasets 45% 11% 94% 78% Bird-Sounds-Global 44% 43% 92% 57% Powdermill (new place) 19% 7% 74% 35% Colombia and Costa Rica (new place) 9% 43% 68% 13%
  • On familiar ground a name on a labelled call can be trusted. More than nine in ten are right.
  • Many boxes lie off any label. On Bird-Sounds-Global and in Colombia and Costa Rica it is 43% of the named boxes. Some may be birds that nobody labelled, others may be wrong. The labels cannot tell which.
  • In a new place a name is a hint. About seven in ten on a labelled call are right, and the model names far fewer boxes. It says bird instead, which is what the class is for.
  • The guess on a bird box is often right on familiar ground, less so elsewhere. The Demo shows it as maybe.
  • Colombia and Costa Rica is the hardest case. Only 29 of its 90 species are among the model's classes. Every other bird there can only be named wrongly or bird.

The label threshold sets the balance. A lower one names more boxes and gets more of them wrong:

The dashed line is the default, 0.25. It scored best on the validation splits for presence per recording (macro F1 0.591 at 0.15, 0.627 at 0.25, 0.617 at 0.35) and for bout-aware matching. --label-conf sets another one.

When names matter most

In a place the model was not trained on, raise --label-conf to 0.45. On Powdermill 92% of the names on a labelled call are then right, and 7% of the boxes get one.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [4] Feng, C., Zhong, Y., Gao, Y., Scott, M. R., & Huang, W. (2021). "TOOD: Task-aligned one-stage object detection." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), 3510–3519.

docs.title: Birds-With-Labels Call Labels
docs.text:
Four of the six training datasets box a whole song. The Birds-With-Labels model should box each call. This page explains how the song labels were turned into call labels that keep their species, for steps 2 and 3 of the training recipe.

The rule builds on Just-Bird's label refinement. Just-Bird has one class, so it only needs to know where the calls are. With species, three questions are new:

  • Whose call is it? Labels of different species often overlap. One call can lie in several of them.
  • What if a species loses its labels? A label whose calls all went to another species would take its clip out of training.
  • What about species the call teacher does not hear? Some species would vanish from the training data.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Dataset Labels What happens Northeastern US, Western US, Amazon Basin per song replaced by call boxes Bird-Sounds-Global mixed, mostly more than one call replaced by call boxes Hawai'i, Southern Sierra Nevada per call kept as they are

Two models work together, and neither is asked a question it cannot answer:

  • The call teacher knows where. It is teacher 2 of the Just-Bird recipe. It has one class and finds calls of any species, down to a confidence of 0.05.
  • The species teacher knows which. It is the previous model, the result of step 1, trained on the human labels. It is asked only where several species are possible.

Neither adds a species of its own. Every call label has a species that a person heard in that clip, at that time and in that frequency band.

flowchart TD
  box["A human box<br/>with a species"]
  q1{"Does the call teacher find a call<br/>at least half inside the box?"}
  q2{"Is the call inside boxes<br/>of several species?"}
  one["The call gets<br/>the species of the box"]
  st["The species teacher<br/>picks one of them"]
  q3{"Is the species protected?"}
  keep["The human box stays"]
  out["The clip is left out"]
  box --> q1
  q1 -- yes --> q2
  q1 -- no --> q3
  q2 -- no --> one
  q2 -- yes --> st
  q3 -- yes --> keep
  q3 -- no --> out

Four clips of the training data, with the human labels, the boxes of the call teacher and the call labels made from them. The human boxes appear dotted in the middle:

  1. One song, one species. The box of the Red-eyed Vireo spans the clip. The call teacher finds its calls, and they all become Red-eyed Vireo. The smaller of two nested boxes is dropped.
  2. Two species at once. The labels of Wood Thrush and Veery overlap. All three calls lie in the Wood Thrush box, and two of them in the Veery box as well. The species teacher gives those two to the Veery.
  3. A protected species. The call teacher finds nothing in the Mountain Quail label. The quail is protected, so its label stays.
  4. Nothing found. The call teacher finds no call in the label. The clip is left out, so that a label over silence teaches nothing.

docs.title: The Rule
docs.text:
For every clip and every human box in it:

  1. Half inside. A box of the call teacher qualifies when at least half of it lies inside the human box. It is trimmed to the human box and takes its species.
  2. Call-sized labels. If no box of the call teacher qualifies for a label of at most 0.5 s, the label takes the box that covers most of it. That box must cover at least half.
  3. One call, several species. The species teacher decides, see below.
  4. Duplicates. Two boxes of one species with an IoU of 0.6 or more are merged. Of two nested boxes of one species, only the larger stays.
  5. Nothing found. If a human box gets no call, its whole clip is left out, with all its labels. Protected species are the exception.

Steps 1, 2, 4 and 5 are Just-Bird's rule, applied to each species on its own. Just-Bird Label Refinement gives the reasons for them.

docs.title: One Call, Several Species
docs.text:
In a dawn chorus the labels of several species cover the same seconds. A call in the overlap fits all of them. If each of them kept it, one call would train two species, and one of them would learn the wrong sound.

  • The species teacher picks. Of the species in question, the call goes to the one with the most confident box of the species teacher over the call.
  • Without an opinion, the fit decides. If the species teacher has no box there, the call goes to the label it lies furthest inside. If two fit equally well, both keep it.
  • No label ends up empty. A label whose calls all went to other species keeps its calls after all. They then carry two species.

Without the species teacher, 60,630 training calls in Northeastern US and 14,350 in Amazon Basin would have carried two species.

docs.title: Protected Species
docs.text:
The call teacher misses some species almost entirely. Most of them have low, tonal calls: doves, tinamous and trogons. The strict rule 5 would leave out their clips, and with them the species.

A species is protected when it would keep less than 25% of its training clips, or fewer than 10 training boxes. Its human box stays where the call teacher found nothing. This applies to 72 species and keeps 14,830 human boxes in the three splits together. A clip with a very rare protected species (fewer than 10 boxes) keeps all its human boxes.

docs.title: What Each Part Saves
docs.text:
Each row adds one part of the rule. The bar spans the middle 80% of the species, and the dot marks the median:

  • Just-Bird's rule alone would remove 16 species from training.
  • The species teacher makes the labels cleaner. It takes calls away from labels, so more clips are left out.
  • Giving lost labels their calls back wins these clips back, and more.
  • Protection keeps every species. Nine in ten species now keep at least 53% of their clips.

docs.title: Box Length
docs.text: The median label shrinks to about half, or to less than a third in Northeastern US and to about a third in Amazon Basin. The model follows its labels. The boxes of Birds-With-Labels on the test split shrink in the same way, before any merging:

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A call outside every human box stays unlabelled, as in the original data. The model learns it as background.
  • A call that the call teacher misses inside a song box loses its label. The model then found some species less often, until distillation repaired it.
  • The tests use the human labels. The test results on these pages compare with the labels people drew, songs included. Call labels of the test clips exist only for the match per dataset.

docs.title: Birds-With-Labels Model Types and Format Parity
docs.text: BirdBox ships two pretrained models, Just-Bird and Birds-With-Labels. Both are released in multiple runtime formats to cover different deployment targets. This page covers the Birds-With-Labels model. It documents every available format and shows how each one compares against the PyTorch baseline on identical recordings, so you can confirm that conversion or quantization does not degrade detection quality.

docs.title: Supported model formats
docs.text:
Each format targets a different deployment scenario. Install the matching runtime with python install.py --model-format <FORMAT>. See Installation for the full setup guide.

Format Typical use case Runtime .pt Default. PyTorch checkpoint, easiest to get started. PyTorch (CUDA or CPU) .onnx Cross-platform deployment, quantized variants available. ONNX Runtime (GPU or CPU) .tflite Edge devices and mobile targets. LiteRT / ai-edge-litert (CPU)

Each format needs an environment with its runtime

An environment runs .pt models and the format it was installed for. Loading a .onnx or .tflite model without its runtime stops with an error that names the install command. Create a separate environment for each format you use and run python install.py --model-format <FORMAT> in it. See Install Parameters for the full table.

docs.title: Verdict criteria
docs.text:
PASS

The model matches at least 90% of baseline detections, adds no more than 10% extra detections, and keeps the mean confidence difference at or below 0.05. The export is safe to use in place of the baseline.

WARN

One or more thresholds were exceeded. The model runs but performance may have degraded after conversion or quantization. Inspect the per-model detail below and compare detections on your own audio before deploying.

FAIL

The worker subprocess exited with an error. The model did not produce any detections. Check the per-model detail below for the full traceback.

docs.title: Metric glossary
docs.text:
Matching is one-to-one and recording by recording: a candidate detection can match a baseline detection of the same species when their 2D IoU (time and frequency) is at least 0.5. Pairs are taken in order of decreasing IoU, and each detection is used at most once.

Metric What it tells you Mean IoU Average time-and-frequency box overlap between matched pairs. 1.000 is a perfect overlap. Lower values mean boxes drifted in position or size. Mean Conf Δ Average absolute confidence difference on matched detections. Near 0.000 means the converted model is as confident as the baseline. Max Conf Δ Largest single confidence difference among matched detections. Surfaces worst-case outliers that the mean hides. Load (s) Wall-clock seconds to load the model file and build the detector. Detect (s) Wall-clock seconds spent running inference on all recordings. The times come from one machine and depend on whether a runtime uses the GPU, so they are not a speed benchmark.

docs.title: Birds-With-Labels Training
docs.text: How the Birds-With-Labels model was trained, in three steps: species from human labels (step 1), call boxes (step 2) and the bird class (step 3). The page also shows what each step changed, the training curves, what else was tried, and the data. Two pages go into detail. Call Labels shows how the training labels were made, and Bird Class and Names how the model finds and names calls.

docs.title: Models and Terms
docs.text:
Three models take part in the three training steps. Two of them are teachers:

Model What it is What it does here Previous model, also called the species teacher when it teaches The result of step 1, a model that draws one box per species over a whole song. Step 2 starts from its weights. A copy that no longer changes is the species teacher. It picks the species of a call when several are possible, and keeps the student from forgetting species in steps 2 and 3. Call teacher Teacher 2 of the Just-Bird recipe. It has one class. Finds the calls inside the human boxes. Student The model being trained in steps 2 and 3. Its best epoch in step 3 is Birds-With-Labels.

These terms are used on this page and on the two detail pages:

Term Meaning Human labels The boxes people drew. Most of them cover a whole song or several calls. The Just-Bird pages call these bout labels. Call labels Mostly one box per call, made from the human labels (see Call Labels). Class score A number between 0 and 1 that the model gives each class, its confidence that the class is there. The scores of the species are the species scores. Position One of the points in the image at which YOLO predicts a box and its class scores, 1,344 in a 256×256 image. Target What the model should have given, a class score or the edges of a box. Loss How far the model's class scores and boxes are from their targets. Training makes it smaller. Distillation Training a student on the class scores of a teacher, in addition to the labels.

docs.title: Training Recipe
docs.text:
The model has to do two things that pull in different directions. It should find every call and box it tightly, as Just-Bird does. And it should know 632 species, many of them from a few dozen examples. The recipe learns these one after the other, and each step starts from the weights of the step before:

flowchart TD
  human["Human labels,<br/>per song and per call<br/>five datasets<br/>+ Bird-Sounds-Global"]
  coco["YOLO11l<br/>COCO weights"]
  jb["Call teacher<br/>(Just-Bird's teacher 2)"]
  s1["Step 1: species<br/>two runs on human labels,<br/>15 + 13 epochs kept"]
  prev["Previous model,<br/>the species teacher"]
  labels["Call labels<br/>one box per call, with species"]
  s2["Step 2: call boxes<br/>10 epochs, with distillation"]
  s3["Step 3: bird class<br/>10 epochs, with distillation"]
  out["Birds-With-Labels<br/>632 species, unknown, bird"]
  coco --> s1
  human --> s1
  s1 --> prev
  prev -- "starting weights" --> s2
  prev -.-> s2
  prev -.-> s3
  prev -- "which species" --> labels
  jb -- "where" --> labels
  human --> labels
  labels --> s2
  labels --> s3
  s2 --> s3
  s3 --> out

Dotted arrows are distillation: the later steps also learn the species scores of the previous model, which keeps them from forgetting species. Solid arrows are everything else that goes into a step, such as weights and labels. The call teacher says where the calls are, and the species teacher says which species they are. Models and Terms explains the names.

Step 1: species Step 2: call boxes Step 3: bird class Starts from COCO weights [18] previous model (step 1) step 2 Labels human call labels call labels Classes 633 633 634, with bird Distillation none from the previous model, weight 2 from the previous model, weight 2 Epochs run 30, then 23 10 10 Learning rate 1e-3, then 8.6e-4 3e-4 3e-4 Kept epoch 15, then 13 10 9 Training time per epoch 21 min 20 min 21 min

All steps train YOLO11l on 256×256 pixel images of 3 s clips, with AdamW, weight decay 0.01 and batches of 64. The augmentation includes mixup [36] and cutmix. Only the first run of step 1 switched them off for its last 10 epochs, after the kept epoch. Mosaic and flips are not used. The images have the rolling noise floor, so the model sees in training what it sees in a recording.

Rare species appear more often in training than in the data. Each epoch repeats an image more often the rarer its rarest species is (repeat-factor sampling [7], threshold 0.001). In steps 2 and 3 this turns 270,949 images into 293,839 per epoch. The rarest are shown up to 12 times.

docs.title: Step 1: Species From Human Labels
docs.text:
The first step learns the species, from the boxes people drew. Its result is the previous model.

  • First run: 30 epochs with a cosine decay of the learning rate. Validation mAP50 on the human labels peaked at epoch 15 (0.416) and fell to 0.393 by epoch 30.
  • Second run: from epoch 15 of the first run. The learning rate goes back up to 8.6e-4 and then decays linearly, by about 1% of that per epoch. So it stays high (7.5e-4 at the kept epoch), while the cosine decay of the first run had already reached 5.6e-4 at epoch 15. Validation mAP50 rose to 0.423 at epoch 13 of this run, and it stopped early after epoch 23.

These values are on the human labels of the val splits. On the call labels, the same model has a validation mAP50 of only 0.232, because it draws song boxes.

Most of these labels box a whole song. So on the song-labelled datasets the previous model draws boxes of 2 to 3 s, over the pauses between the calls as well.

docs.title: Step 2: Call Boxes Without Forgetting Species
docs.text:
The second step replaces the song boxes with call boxes. The call teacher finds the calls inside each human box, and each call takes the species of that box. Call Labels explains the rule.

The step does two things. The call labels change the shape of the boxes. Distillation keeps the species while that happens.

docs.title: What the Call Labels Change
docs.text:
The call labels alone turn song boxes into call boxes. Here the previous model is compared with the same model trained on the call labels without distillation, with distillation, and after step 3:

Previous model Call labels, no distillation Call labels, distillation After step 3 (released) Match with the call labels (mAP50-95) 0.094 0.282 0.247 0.256 Median box length, Northeastern US test 2.99 s 0.65 s 1.26 s 0.56 s Presence, 3 s segments (macro F1) 0.515 0.492 0.516 0.512

The match is the mAP50-95 on the val splits with the call labels. Distillation uses weight 2. What Distillation Protects compares the tests.

  • The call labels reshape the boxes. Without distillation the match triples, and the boxes shrink to about a fifth.
  • Distillation keeps the species. It gives up part of the new shape for them. The match falls from 0.282 to 0.247, and the boxes get longer, from 0.65 s to 1.26 s.
  • Step 3 tightens the boxes again. They end at 0.56 s, close to the call labels (0.65 s on the same split).

The change is largest where the human labels are longer than one call. The table shows mAP50-95 on the test clips, without distillation. Call labels were made for the test clips too, but only for this comparison. All other tests use the human labels:

Dataset Human labels Match with call labels: previous → new Match with human labels: previous → new Northeastern US per song 0.027 → 0.351 0.289 → 0.024 Western US per song 0.063 → 0.380 0.218 → 0.033 Amazon Basin per song 0.132 → 0.280 0.304 → 0.118 Bird-Sounds-Global mixed, mostly more than one call 0.086 → 0.278 0.182 → 0.059 Hawai'i per call 0.273 → 0.277 same labels Southern Sierra Nevada per call 0.247 → 0.238 same labels

Song boxes and call boxes cannot both match. So a model that draws call boxes loses against the human song labels, even if every call is right. The two datasets labelled per call stay level, because the previous model already drew call boxes there.

Why the match triples and presence barely moves. The two scores ask different questions and use different labels. Take a song of 3 s with six calls of 0.3 s:

Previous model: one box of 3 s New model: six call boxes Match with the six call labels none found, the IoU is at most 0.1 all six found Presence, 3 s segments right right Bout-aware, either way right right

The previous model already knew the species and only drew the box differently. So the species tests that ignore box shape have little to gain. The numbers fit this:

  • The stricter the overlap, the larger the gain. Without distillation, mAP50 rises from 0.232 to 0.438 (1.9 times) and mAP50-95 from 0.094 to 0.282 (3 times).
  • Where the labels did not change, nothing is gained. Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada stay level. If the model named species better in general, they should rise too.

So the rise of the match is mostly new box shapes. It does not show that the model names species better. Step 2 alone also covers no more of Just-Bird's boxes in the 14 soundscapes from other places. It covers 31% of them, as the previous model does. The jump comes with step 3.

What the Match Can Tell

The call labels come from the call teacher, which trained on some of these clips. So the match measures agreement with the call teacher, not with people. The independent test is Powdermill, labelled by people in a new place. There F1 for finding calls at IoU 0.25 rises from 0.277 for the previous model to 0.656 for the released model, which includes step 3.

docs.title: What Distillation Protects
docs.text:
Training on the call labels alone makes the model worse at some species. Where the call teacher finds only a few calls of a song, the rest of that song becomes background. The model then learns to ignore the species there. The species are not gone, but some are found less often.

Distillation repairs this [10]. The species teacher looks at the same image, and its species scores become a second target. The labels say where the calls are, and the species teacher says which species are heard. Training a model on new labels while holding it to the answers it gave before is known as learning without forgetting [17].

The loss of the class scores has two parts:

\[ L_{\text{cls}} = \underbrace{\text{BCE}(\text{student}, \text{call labels})}_{\text{match the call labels}} + w \cdot \underbrace{\text{KL}(\text{species teacher} \,\|\, \text{student})}_{\text{stay close to the previous model}} \]

BCE is binary cross-entropy, the usual classification loss of YOLO. At every position, the model answers one yes-or-no question per class: is this an Ovenbird? Is this a Veery? For a score \(p\) and a target \(y\) the loss is

\[ \text{BCE}(p, y) = -\big[\, y \log p + (1 - y) \log (1 - p) \,\big] \]

Say the target is 1. A score of 0.9 then costs 0.11, and a score of 0.1 costs 2.30. YOLO's own targets for a call lie between 0 and 1. They are higher where the predicted box fits the label better, and 0 at positions without a label.

KL is the Kullback-Leibler divergence. It measures how far the student's score \(p\) is from the score \(q\) of the species teacher. It is 0 when they agree:

\[ \text{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \text{BCE}(p, q) - \text{BCE}(q, q) \]

It is computed at every position and for each of the 633 classes, in steps 2 and 3. At the start of step 2 it is 0, because the student still equals the species teacher. The new class bird of step 3 has no KL part. The box loss uses the call labels only.

An example. An Ovenbird sings, but the call teacher misses one of the bird's calls, so this call has no label. BCE alone then teaches that nothing is there. The species teacher still hears the Ovenbird, so KL pulls the class score back up. At weight 2 the two balance at two thirds of the species teacher's score.

The weight \(w\) sets how much the species teacher counts. Five runs were compared. The figure has three plots, one below the other, with the weight at the bottom:

  • Plot A: how well the species are found, as the change against the previous model.
  • Plot B: how well the boxes match the call labels.
  • Plot C: how long the boxes are.

Weight 0 means no distillation at all. All five runs train on the call labels, also the one at weight 0. So the step from the previous model to weight 0 is what the call labels do. The way from weight 0 to the right is what distillation does.

Seen from weight 0, distillation wins back species in plot A. It costs some of the match in plot B, and the boxes get longer in plot C. The large rise in plot B, from 0.094 to 0.282, comes from the call labels alone. Plot A has three tests, and plot B has the match with the call labels. All four need the right species. They differ in the place and shape of the box, and in the labels they compare with:

Test What counts as right Place Box shape Compared with Presence, 3 s segments The species is detected and labelled in the segment. Detected but not labelled counts as wrong. only the segment ignored human labels, test Bout-aware, either way A box of the species lies at least half inside the label, or the label at least half inside the box. roughly ignored human labels, test Box by box, IoU 0.25 A box and a label of one species overlap with an IoU of at least 0.25. A label can match only one box. yes loosely human labels, test Match (mAP50-95) As box by box, but at ten IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95, on 3 s clips and without merging boxes. yes strictly call labels, val

All four use the five datasets and Bird-Sounds-Global together. The scores are calculated in two ways:

  • Macro F1 (the first three) is the F1 of each species at one confidence threshold, averaged over the species. The threshold is chosen on the val splits with the human labels, for each model and test.
  • mAP50-95 (the match) is the average precision of each class over all confidence thresholds, averaged over the classes and the ten IoU thresholds. The classes are the species and the class unknown.

So the match also needs the right species. Its rise comes mostly from the shape of the boxes, as explained above.

An example. In the song of 3 s from above, the human label is one box. The model draws six correct call boxes of 0.3 s in it, as tall as the label.

  • Presence: right, the species is found in the segment.
  • Bout-aware: right, the label is found.
  • Box by box: each call box covers a tenth of the label, so its IoU is 0.1. The label counts as missed, and all six boxes count as wrong.
  • Match: right, because it compares with the call labels. Each box has its own.

Why box by box falls while the match rises. They compare with different labels, and call boxes cannot match both. Box by box uses the human labels, which mostly box a whole song. The match uses the call labels, one box per call. The table per dataset shows it with the same score on the same clips. On Northeastern US, mAP50-95 rises from 0.027 to 0.351 against the call labels. Against the human labels it falls from 0.289 to 0.024. So box by box falls mostly because the boxes change shape, and this is what raises the match.

Box by box loses much less than mAP50-95 on the human labels, 0.073 of 0.406. There are three likely reasons, which were not measured one by one:

  • Boxes are merged first. The merge is chosen on the val splits with the human labels. It joins part of the call boxes into songs again.
  • An IoU of 0.25 is loose. mAP50-95 needs at least 0.5, and at 0.5 box by box loses more as well (0.310 to 0.202).
  • Not every label is a song of several calls. Labels per call and songs without pauses lose little or nothing.

Not all of the 0.073 is shape. Without distillation the model also finds some species less often, as presence shows (−0.022). At weight 2 presence is back, but box by box still loses 0.025. This rest is mostly shape.

How to read plot A. Each value is the change of macro F1 against the previous model, which is the line at 0. The points at weight 0 show the call labels alone, so comparing the others with them shows what distillation does. It wins back all of the loss in the first two tests, and two thirds of it box by box:

Test Previous model Without distillation Weight 2 Presence, 3 s segments 0.515 −0.022 +0.001 Bout-aware, either way 0.477 −0.015 +0.003 Box by box, IoU 0.25 0.406 −0.073 −0.025

How to read plots B and C. Weight 0 is the call labels alone, without distillation. From there the match with the call labels falls with every weight, from 0.282 to 0.229, and the boxes get longer. Both stay far from the previous model (0.094 in plot B, 2.99 s in plot C) even at weight 4. So distillation gives up part of the new shape, but does not undo it.

  • Without distillation (weight 0) the boxes are tightest. The species tests that ignore box shape lose only 0.015 to 0.022. Training still starts from the previous model, and every call label carries its species.
  • Up to weight 2 this loss disappears. At 2, presence and bout-aware matching are level with the previous model.
  • At weight 4 precision falls, and the boxes get longer. The model drifts back to the previous one.
  • Box by box (dashed in plot A) is mostly about box shape, as in the example. It stays below the previous model at every weight, because that model draws song boxes. It is highest at weight 4, partly because the boxes are longer there. So it is no reason for a weight above 2. On the two datasets labelled per call, weight 0 is level with the previous model (0.488 for both at IoU 0.5).

Weight 2 is the balance: the species are level with the previous model, and the boxes are much closer to call boxes than to song boxes. The boxes it draws are still longer than the call labels, 1.26 s against 0.65 s. Step 3 closes that gap.

docs.title: Which Species Are Found Less Often
docs.text:
The average hides that the loss is uneven. It is largest for species whose songs have few call labels. The table groups the 495 species of the presence test by the share of the time of their human boxes that the call labels cover. Recall is the share of labelled 3 s segments in which the species is found. The values are the mean change against the previous model:

Covered by call labels Species Recall without distillation Recall at weight 2 up to 30% 32 −0.177 −0.034 30 to 45% 86 −0.062 −0.004 45 to 60% 163 −0.034 −0.008 60 to 75% 158 −0.021 0.000 above 75% 56 −0.013 −0.009 all 495 −0.041 −0.007

The loss is one of recall. Precision changes little on average, by −0.002 without distillation and +0.006 at weight 2.

docs.title: Step 3: The Bird Class
docs.text:
After step 2 the model boxes calls and knows its species. But in 14 soundscapes from other places it covered only a third of the boxes Just-Bird draws. Just-Bird learns one class from every box. Here each species class learns from its own boxes, half of the species from fewer than 134.

The third step adds a class bird that every box trains, whatever its species. Its score finds the calls, and the species scores name them. Bird Class and Names explains both.

docs.title: What Each Step Changes
docs.text:
• Calls in 14 soundscapes: the bird class brings the jump, from 31% to 76% of Just-Bird's boxes. The soundscapes come from places outside the training data. No human labels exist for them, so Just-Bird's boxes are the reference, right or wrong. Each model runs at its own threshold. Two sets with human labels are tested in Performance in New Places.
  • Box length: each step makes the boxes shorter. The 1.26 s after step 2 include distillation. The released model's are as long as Just-Bird's (0.56 s on Northeastern US for both).
  • Species: both tests that ignore the shape of the boxes stay nearly level. By these two tests, finding and boxing calls costs almost nothing in species. The last bar of each is the released model as BirdBox ships it, with names at a species score of 0.25.

Box by box gets lower, and the figure does not show it. On the human labels of the five datasets and Bird-Sounds-Global together, macro F1 at IoU 0.25 falls with each step:

Previous model Step 2 Step 3 (released) Box by box, IoU 0.25 0.406 0.381 0.339 Change against the previous model −0.025 −0.067

Most of this is box shape, as explained above. One more part comes from the merge: BirdBox merges the boxes of the released model without looking at their species. So it cannot join the calls of one species into a song. With boxes merged per species and thresholds on the species score, the value is 0.367.

docs.title: Training Results
docs.text:
The figure shows the validation mAP of the species, the box loss and the classification loss after each epoch of steps 2 and 3. The validation set is the val splits with the call labels. The dashed line marks the start of the bird class, which adds its own term to the classification loss. The dots at 0 are the previous model on the same call labels, so most of the rise comes in the first epoch.

The validation classification loss lies above the training loss, and this is not overfitting: it still falls in both runs. The gap is the KL part. Without distillation the two end at 1.51 and 1.40, and the gap grows with the weight, to 2.36 at weight 2. A likely cause is batch normalization. In validation the student uses its stored statistics, while the species teacher uses those of the batch.

Model Checkpoint

Each run kept the weights with the highest mAP50-95 on the validation split: epoch 10 of the call-box run (0.247) and epoch 9 of the bird-class run (0.256), which is epoch 19 in the figure.

docs.title: What Else Was Tried
docs.text: Idea Result Train on the call labels from COCO weights, 30 epochs and a second run About the same on calls as fine-tuning for 10 epochs, and a larger loss in presence (−0.034 and −0.031 against −0.022, all without distillation) Keep the previous model and take the boxes from Just-Bird at inference Keeps the species and draws call boxes, but needs two models per run Lower learning rate on the call labels (1e-4), without distillation Level on every test, slightly looser boxes Let Just-Bird's scores teach the bird class in step 3 Covers more of Just-Bird's boxes in the 14 soundscapes (82% against 76%), but more boxes lie elsewhere (11% against 7%), and the validation mAP50-95 of the species falls from 0.256 to 0.247 Start step 1 from an earlier model of the five datasets, not from COCO weights Learns the Bird-Sounds-Global species much worse (validation mAP50 on the human labels of that dataset 0.305 against 0.356), and the species of the five datasets slightly better (0.537 against 0.530)

docs.title: Data Splits
docs.text:
The model trains on the train splits, picks its checkpoint on the val splits and is tested on the test splits, about 70/15/15 (see Dataset Splits). The val splits are used twice. The checkpoints of steps 2 and 3 are picked with the call labels, the thresholds and merges of the tests with the human labels. The tests themselves use the human labels. Boxes and images of the training split, counted per 3 s clip. Consecutive clips overlap by half, so most calls are counted twice:

Dataset Human labels Clips, step 1 Boxes, step 1 Clips, steps 2 and 3 Boxes, steps 2 and 3 Northeastern US per song 116,866 151,396 108,824 230,902 Western US per song 35,082 55,835 27,212 48,350 Amazon Basin per song 30,801 79,086 19,342 66,223 Bird-Sounds-Global mixed 84,404 125,354 70,879 134,104 Hawai'i per call 33,496 63,261 33,496 63,261 Southern Sierra Nevada per call 11,196 16,528 11,196 16,528 All 311,845 491,460 270,949 559,368

Northeastern US has fewer clips and more boxes after step 1, because one song box becomes several call boxes. Amazon Basin loses the most clips. Its recordings are dense choruses with long, overlapping labels, and the call teacher often finds no call for one of them.

docs.title: Birds-With-Labels Model
docs.text:
The Birds-With-Labels model combines all five zenodo datasets mentioned in the introduction with Bird-Sounds-Global, annotated soundscapes from xeno-canto. The five datasets bring almost 407 hours of soundscape recordings with 155,584 bounding box labels of 281 bird species. Bird-Sounds-Global adds 111 hours with 62,030 labels of 765 species from many countries. The model has 634 classes: the 281 species of the five datasets, the 351 Bird-Sounds-Global species with at least 10 training labels in at least 3 recordings, the class unknown for the rest, and bird for calls of any species. Annotation files write unknown as ???? (see Labels of unknown species).

It finds calls as Just-Bird does, with one tight box per call, and names each box after its species when it is sure. Otherwise the box is named bird. Species Names explains how.

Eight seconds from Powdermill, a place the model was not trained on. White boxes are named bird. The model boxes six of the seven labelled vocalizations, names two of them correctly and leaves the others as bird. It also boxes five short sounds at 5 to 8 kHz that have no label. The previous model draws four boxes of several seconds.

More on Birds-With-Labels:

  • Training: the three training steps and what each of them changed, training curves, and boxes per species and split.
  • Call Labels: how the song labels were split into call labels that keep their species.
  • Bird Class and Names: how the model finds calls and names them, and how far the names can be trusted.
  • Model Types: the export formats and how closely they match the PyTorch model.

The detections behind the scores of Birds-With-Labels come from BirdBox as it ships: the rolling noise floor (each test minute after the audio before it) and names at a species score of 0.25. Merge and threshold differ, and each section says which ones it uses. Chosen on val means the ones that score best on the val splits with the human labels. All test labels are the human labels.

docs.title: Finding Calls
docs.text:
With species ignored, the model finds calls as well as Just-Bird. Every box and every label counts as bird, so F1 measures finding calls alone. Both models use Just-Bird's NMS (IoU 0.5) and the merge and threshold that score best on val.

Test set Just-Bird Birds-With-Labels Five datasets, IoU 0.25 0.404 0.412 Five datasets, IoU 0.5 0.223 0.235 Bird-Sounds-Global, IoU 0.25 0.367 0.377 Bird-Sounds-Global, IoU 0.5 0.195 0.197 Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada (labelled per call), IoU 0.5 0.558 0.576 Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada (labelled per call), IoU 0.75 0.297 0.291

Just-Bird was trained on the test splits of Birds-With-Labels too, so it has seen these recordings. On 14 soundscapes from other places no human labels exist, so Just-Bird's boxes (confidence 0.15) serve as the reference. The model draws about as many boxes, covers 76% of Just-Bird's (each by at least half of its duration), and 7% of its boxes lie elsewhere. The previous model covered 31%.

docs.title: Performance in New Places
docs.text:
Two sets with human boxes come from none of the training sources. They show how the model does in places it was not trained on:

  • Powdermill, Pennsylvania (Chronister et al.): 6.4 hours of morning recordings with 16,052 boxes. 40 of its 48 species are among the model's classes.
  • Colombia and Costa Rica (Vega-Hidalgo et al.): 34 hours on coffee farms with 7,338 boxes. 29 of its 90 species are among the model's classes.

Finding calls. F1 with species ignored, each model at its default threshold and merge, with NMS at IoU 0.5:

Test set Just-Bird Previous model Birds-With-Labels Powdermill, IoU 0.25 0.620 0.277 0.656 Powdermill, IoU 0.5 0.415 0.112 0.465 Colombia and Costa Rica, IoU 0.25 0.172 0.173 0.182 Colombia and Costa Rica, IoU 0.5 0.071 0.066 0.078

Precision and recall at IoU 0.25 over all confidence thresholds. The dots are the default thresholds:

  • The model finds calls at least as well as Just-Bird in both places.
  • The default threshold carries over. On Powdermill the best threshold and merge would gain only 0.001 at IoU 0.25.
  • Colombia and Costa Rica is sparsely labelled. It has 3.6 labels per minute against 42 on Powdermill, and 27% of the model's boxes with a score of at least 0.7 lie more than 0.5 s from any label. So many boxes count as wrong for every model, and only the comparison tells something.

Names carry over less. On Powdermill 19% of the boxes get a name. Of the named boxes on a call of a labelled species, 74% are right. On the test splits of the five datasets it is 45% and 94%. How Reliable Are the Names has all numbers.

docs.title: Species
docs.text:
Two kinds of test tell apart how well the model names species and how well its boxes match the labels. Most labels of the five datasets and Bird-Sounds-Global box a whole song, while the model boxes each call. Thresholds are chosen on val. The box-by-box tests also choose the merge on val, the others use the boxes before merging.

Which species are there, and where. These tests barely depend on the shape of the boxes, except boxes inside a label. Presence compares the species detected in each 3 s segment or whole recording with the species labelled there. A species that is detected but not labelled counts as wrong. Bout-aware matching counts a label as found when boxes of its species lie inside it, and a box as correct when it lies inside a label of its species. At least half of the box has to lie inside. Either way also accepts a label that lies at least half inside a box. Macro F1 over the labelled species of the five datasets and Bird-Sounds-Global together:

Test Previous model Birds-With-Labels Presence, 3 s segments 0.515 0.512 Presence, whole recordings 0.610 0.621 Bout-aware, boxes inside a label 0.440 0.477 Bout-aware, either way 0.477 0.486

The model names species as well as the previous one: presence and either way change by −0.003 to +0.011. The gain of boxes inside a label (0.440 to 0.477) is partly shape, because a short call box fits into a label more easily than a song box.

Box by box. Each box has to overlap a label of its species at the given IoU:

Test set Previous model Birds-With-Labels Five datasets, IoU 0.25 0.524 0.389 Bird-Sounds-Global, IoU 0.25 0.337 0.304 Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada (labelled per call), IoU 0.5 0.488 0.492 Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada (labelled per call), IoU 0.75 0.247 0.260

On labels per call the model is level with the previous one, at IoU 0.75 as well: the interval of the difference includes 0. On song labels it scores lower: one song label meets several call boxes, and at most one of them can match it.

Boxes named bird are not counted in these tests. They claim a call, not a species.

docs.title: Precision, Recall and F1-Score
docs.text:
The graph below shows precision, recall and F1 on the test splits against the confidence threshold, each averaged over the species with test labels (macro average), at IoU 0.25. The boxes are merged as BirdBox ships, by window fusion with a 0.05 s phrase gap, and the best threshold is read off the test split. So the values differ a little from the box-by-box table above. The upper plot is the test split of the five datasets, the lower one the test split of Bird-Sounds-Global. The confidence is the bird score, so the threshold decides which calls are found. Which of them get a species name is decided by the species score. Both test splits are labelled mostly per song, so the scores are lower than on call labels (see Species). The default threshold is 0.21.

Average over the labelled species

The F-beta analysis (f_beta_score_analysis.py) also averages over species that have detections but no test labels, each with an F1 of 0 (Overall_Macro). A model with more classes has more of them, so this page averages over the labelled species only: 184 in the test split of the five datasets, 357 in Bird-Sounds-Global.

Starting at 0.05

The test detections were made at a confidence of 0.05, so the curves start there.

docs.title: Top Performing Species
docs.text: The figure shows the F1-score against the confidence threshold for the 12 best species among the 82 with at least 50 labels in the test split of the five datasets. Species with fewer labels are left out: with only a few labels, a high F1 is mostly chance. The 12 species reach a best F1 of 0.78 to 0.95.

docs.title: Just-Bird Label Refinement
docs.text:
Most training datasets of the Just-Bird model put one box around a whole song or bout, while the model should draw one box per call. Such boxes also cover the pauses between the calls. A study on crowd-sourced bird recordings found the same problem with labels that cover whole clips, and turned them into call-level labels [2]. Before training, those boxes are replaced by call boxes from a teacher model, in two rounds (see Training Recipe). This page explains the rule, what each round changes, and which boxes and clips are discarded.

The page describes the labels of the released model. Its teachers see log-floor spectrograms, like the model itself. Three design decisions were tested with an earlier version of the recipe, whose teachers and models saw PCEN spectrograms: the looser rule for call-sized boxes, dropping nested boxes, and stopping after two rounds. These tests are marked as such. PCEN or Log-Floor Teachers compares the two kinds of teacher.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The refinement changes only the four bout-labelled datasets: Northeastern US, Western US, Amazon Basin and Bird-Sounds-Global. Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada keep their human call labels (Which Datasets Are Refined explains why). It works on the training images, 3 s clips that overlap by half. An annotation longer than a clip is cut into one box per clip, and each of these boxes is handled on its own.

Terms used on this page:

  • Human box: a box an annotator drew. In these four datasets it usually covers a whole song or bout of several seconds.
  • Replaced: the teacher found at least one call box for the human box, and those call boxes take its place. A human box can be replaced by many call boxes or by one.
  • Discarded: the teacher found no call box that qualifies (see the rule below), so the human box cannot be replaced. It is not used as the annotator drew it either: the human box and its whole 3 s clip are discarded from training, including any other boxes in that clip. Training on long bout boxes made the model worse on a new site (F1 0.124 against 0.383 with call labels, see Each Step on the Unseen Site), so none is kept. Leaving out training samples whose labels cannot be trusted is a common way to learn from noisy labels (sample selection, [31]).
  • Call-sized: the whole annotation, before it was cut into clips, is at most 0.5 s long. That is the median length of the Hawai'i call boxes in the 3 s training clips. Whole Hawai'i annotations have a median of 0.60 s (table below), because an annotation cut at a clip edge leaves shorter boxes. Here the annotator boxed a single call. Longer annotations cover a phrase, song or bout. They are 96% of the boxes in these four datasets.

docs.title: Which Datasets Are Refined
docs.text:
The datasets differ in what one human box covers. In each, every box was traced back to the whole annotation it was cut from (training split, boxes counted per 3 s clip):

Dataset What one box covers Median annotation length Boxes from call-sized annotations Refined Hawai'i a call 0.60 s 47% no Southern Sierra Nevada a call 0.40 s 55% no Bird-Sounds-Global mixed: calls, songs, bouts 2.08 s 7% yes Western US a bout 3.30 s 1% yes Northeastern US a bout 5.50 s 4% yes Amazon Basin a bout 12.80 s 1% yes

The annotation guidelines of Northeastern US, Western US and Amazon Basin let annotators join consecutive calls with pauses under 5 s into one box. The guidelines of Southern Sierra Nevada have no such clause, and Hawai'i is labelled per call as well. Bird-Sounds-Global, soundscapes from xeno-canto, mixes both styles; most of its boxes cover more than one call.

Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada are left as they are, for four reasons:

  • There is nothing to split. About half of their boxes are call-sized, and the median annotation is at most 0.6 s. The rule exists to cut long bout boxes into calls.
  • The rule would lose good labels. A call box the teacher finds is replaced by about the same box, so nothing is gained. A call box the teacher misses is discarded with its whole clip, like the valid faint call below. On call-level labels the rule can only cost data.
  • Hawai'i defines what a call box is. Teacher 1 learned from the Hawai'i labels. Relabelling them with a model trained on them would only feed the teacher's own mistakes back into the training data.
  • Southern Sierra Nevada was the unseen test site while the recipe was developed (see Training Recipe). Its labels had to stay human to measure the teachers and models against. The released model adds them unchanged.

docs.title: The Rule
docs.text:
For every clip:

  1. The teacher proposes boxes with a confidence of at least 0.05. The cutoff is low on purpose: inside a box a human drew, even a weak detection is likely a call. Self-training for object detection usually keeps only confident boxes, because low-confidence boxes are often false positives and would become false labels anywhere in the image [19], [29]. Here the human box limits where a teacher box can go, so a weak box inside it is much less likely to be wrong.
  2. Half-inside test: a teacher box qualifies for a human box when at least half of the teacher box lies within the human box. Small call boxes inside a bout box pass easily.
  3. Looser rule for call-sized boxes: if no teacher box passes the half-inside test and the human box is call-sized, the teacher box that covers the largest share of the human box qualifies, if it covers at least half of it.
  4. The qualifying teacher boxes replace the human box. They are trimmed to its edges, so a new box never leaves the time and frequency range the annotator marked.
  5. Near-duplicates (IoU ≥ 0.6, for example one call inside two overlapping human boxes) are merged, keeping the more confident box.
  6. If no teacher box qualifies, the human box is discarded, and with it the whole clip.
  7. Nested boxes: after both rounds, of two boxes where one lies at least 80% inside the other, the inner one is dropped (Nested Boxes).

The half-inside test is measured on the teacher box, which makes it strict with tight call boxes. The teacher often draws a slightly larger box around the same call. Then less than half of the teacher box lies inside the tight human box (middle), and without the looser rule a good label would be discarded with its clip. The looser rule (bottom) keeps it.

Real clips from the training data. All teacher boxes in the figure are from teacher 2, the second round, whose labels the released model was trained on:

In the first four clips the human box is replaced:

  • a bout box by its call boxes (the nested ones are dropped later, see Nested Boxes)
  • a call box that already fits its call by about the same box
  • a loose call box by a tighter one
  • a tight call box by the trimmed teacher box, under the looser rule

In the last three it is discarded with its clip, for the reasons in Why Boxes Are Discarded:

  • Teacher boxes stick out (Western US): discarded in round 1 and in round 2. The annotation is 1.9 s long, so the looser rule does not apply.
  • Valid faint call (Amazon Basin): the human box is correct, but discarded in round 1 and in round 2. Neither teacher finds the call, even with the confidence cutoff lowered from 0.05 to 0.001: no box of teacher 1 or teacher 2 even touches the human box. So the clip and its good label are lost to training. This is the price of the rule: a call that no teacher detects cannot be told apart from a stretch of silence inside a long annotation, and both are discarded.
  • Quiet stretch (Amazon Basin): a clip from a 12 s annotation. Neither teacher finds a call in this part of it, so it is discarded in both rounds.

Two things the rule cannot do:

  • It never adds a label. A call outside every human box stays unlabelled, as in the original data.
  • A call the teacher misses inside a bout box loses its label, because the call boxes replace the whole bout box. In the bout clip above, the short, low sound at about 0.45 s gets no box in either round and now counts as background. A lower confidence cutoff would find more of these calls, but would also accept more noise.

docs.title: What Each Round Changes
docs.text:
Boxes are counted per 3 s clip here, so no box is longer than 3 s. Round 1 cuts the median box length from 1.15–3.0 s to 0.42–1.10 s, and round 2 to 0.38–0.84 s, close to the 0.50 s of the call-level Hawai'i labels. The larger effect of round 2 is that it replaces more of the bout boxes, so far fewer clips are discarded. Round 2 also applies the looser rule for call-sized boxes.

Dataset Training clips Discarded, round 1 Discarded, round 2 Used for training Northeastern US 116,780 16,731 (14%) 7,525 (6%) 109,255 Western US 36,435 10,724 (29%) 7,639 (21%) 28,796 Amazon Basin 31,264 22,488 (72%) 16,315 (52%) 14,949 Bird-Sounds-Global 84,404 21,838 (26%) 13,638 (16%) 70,766

Round 2 does not build on the labels of round 1. Both rounds start again from the original human boxes, so teacher 2 gets a new chance at every clip that round 1 discarded. Teacher 2 never trained on those clips (it was trained on the round-1 labels, without the discarded clips), but it learned from far more data than teacher 1, which saw only Hawai'i. Comparing the discarded clips of the two rounds:

Dataset Discarded, round 1 Kept again in round 2 Discarded in both rounds Kept in round 1, discarded in round 2 Northeastern US 16,731 9,461 7,270 255 Western US 10,724 3,175 7,549 90 Amazon Basin 22,488 6,404 16,084 231 Bird-Sounds-Global 21,838 8,690 13,148 490 All four 71,781 27,730 (39%) 44,051 1,066

Teacher 2 finds the calls in 39% of the clips that round 1 discarded. Only 1,066 clips go the other way. A call that neither teacher finds, like the faint call above, stays discarded.

docs.title: Why There Is No Third Round
docs.text:
A third round would train teacher 3 on the round-2 labels and relabel again. It was not run, because round 2 already brought no gain on full recordings of the unseen site. This was decided with the PCEN version of the recipe, before the looser rule and dropping nested boxes:

Labels of the bout-labelled datasets F1 at IoU 0.5, unseen site, at the Hawai'i-val threshold Discarded clips Human boxes 0.124 none Round 1 0.381* 87,008 Round 2 0.383 53,066

* This model (teacher 2) was trained on a quarter of the data, the other two on all of it.

  • Round 1 brought the big step, from bout boxes to call boxes.
  • Round 2 ties round 1 on full recordings. Its gains lie elsewhere: 33,942 more clips are kept (19% more bout-labelled training data), 3 s clips score higher, and the threshold chosen on Hawai'i val carries over to the new site.
  • A third round could only win back clips from the 52,174 discarded in both rounds (44,051 with the released model's labels), many of them silent stretches of long annotations. Winning back 1,604 of them with the looser rule moved no score beyond what another training seed would.

A third round was not tested, so this is a judgment from the trend, not a measurement. Each round needs a new teacher, a relabelling of all four datasets and a final training to measure it.

Amazon Basin loses the most. Its recordings are dense choruses with long, overlapping annotations, and even after round 2 about half of its clips are discarded.

docs.title: Why Boxes Are Discarded
docs.text:
A discarded box is not one the teacher judged to be correct: when the teacher finds the call in a good call box, it replaces it with about the same box (the second real clip above). A human box is discarded only when no teacher box qualifies, for one of two reasons:

  • No teacher box. The teacher finds nothing in the box. Usually this is a stretch of a long annotation where the bird is silent or barely audible in this clip, or a faint call.
  • The teacher box sticks out. Teacher boxes touch the human box, but less than half of each lies inside it. This happens where boxes of several birds overlap, as in the Amazon Basin choruses. For a call-sized box it also means that no teacher box covers half of it.

To see which boxes these are, every human box was traced back to the whole annotation it was cut from, and the teacher was run again on every clip with a discarded box:

Dataset Human boxes Call-sized Discarded, all boxes Discarded, call-sized Call-sized share of the discarded boxes Northeastern US 151,983 5,423 (3.6%) 5% 10% 7% Western US 54,951 316 (0.6%) 16% 48% 2% Amazon Basin 77,792 733 (0.9%) 30% 44% 1% Bird-Sounds-Global 125,370 8,467 (6.8%) 13% 15% 8% All four 410,096 14,939 (3.6%) 14% 15% 4%

Round 2, training split, boxes counted per 3 s clip.

  • Call-sized boxes are discarded about as often as longer ones over all four datasets (15% against 14%). The looser rule keeps most call-sized boxes whose teacher box sticks out. In 70% of the call-sized boxes that are still discarded, the teacher found nothing.
  • In Western US and Amazon Basin, call-sized boxes are still discarded more often (48% and 44%). There, too, the teacher finds nothing in most of them (83–84%).
  • Call-sized boxes are rare. These datasets were annotated per bout, and only 3.6% of their boxes are call-sized. They make up 4% of the discarded boxes.
  • Most discarded boxes come from long annotations. In 48% of them the teacher found nothing, mostly silent or faint stretches. In the rest its boxes stick out, above all in Amazon Basin (60% of its discarded boxes).

docs.title: The Looser Rule for Call-Sized Boxes
docs.text:
The half-inside test rejects good call boxes whenever the teacher draws a larger box. For call-sized human boxes only, the looser rule (step 3 of the rule) also accepts a teacher box that covers at least half of the human box. It is trimmed to the human box, so the label stays about the same as the annotator drew it, and the clip stays in training. In short: if the teacher confirms there is a call, the clip is kept.

The rule was tested with the PCEN version of the recipe, on the Southern Sierra Nevada hold-out. There it keeps 1,604 clips that the half-inside test alone discards, 0.6% more bout-labelled training data. A model trained with them, with the recipe otherwise unchanged, scores:

Rule Unseen site, IoU 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75, best threshold Unseen site, IoU 0.5 at the Hawai'i-val threshold Hawai'i val, IoU 0.5, best threshold Half-inside test only 0.541 / 0.384 / 0.116 0.383 0.584 With the looser rule 0.541 / 0.389 / 0.120 0.387 0.586

Every score is the same or up to 0.005 higher, no more than a second training run with another seed moves it (0.001–0.006, see Nested Boxes). Discarding these clips costs nothing measurable, and keeping them does no harm: a manual check of some of the kept clips found real calls in the human boxes, with teacher boxes far larger than the call around them. The released model uses the looser rule (--call-cover 0.5 in refine_coarse_boxes.py).

docs.title: Nested Boxes in the Refined Labels
docs.text:
In the round-2 labels, about half of the boxes of the four refined datasets lie at least 80% inside a larger box of the same clip. Nearly all of these pairs lie inside one human box: teacher 2 often draws a phrase box and the syllable boxes inside it, and both qualify. The merge in step 5 of the rule only catches near-duplicates (IoU ≥ 0.6), not a small box inside a large one. Window fusion removes nested boxes from the model's output, and step 7 removes them from the training labels in the same way: it drops the inner box of each pair (drop inner).

Dataset Human labels: boxes inside a larger box Round 2: boxes dropped as nested Hawai'i 2% not refined Southern Sierra Nevada 1% not refined Northeastern US 13% 57% Western US 3% 63% Amazon Basin 26% 51% Bird-Sounds-Global 3% 56%

Training split, boxes counted per 3 s clip. A box counts as nested when at least 80% of it lies inside a larger box.

Drop inner keeps the phrase box of each pair. The other choice, drop outer, keeps the syllable boxes. Both were tested with the PCEN version of the recipe, each against the round-2 labels with no nested boxes dropped. That recipe was also trained a second time with another seed, to measure the noise of one run. Full recordings, window fusion as BirdBox runs it, phrase gap off:

Labels Unseen site, IoU 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75, best threshold Hawai'i val, IoU 0.5, best threshold Round 2, nested boxes kept 0.541 / 0.384 / 0.116 0.584 Round 2, nested boxes kept, second seed 0.543 / 0.390 / 0.115 0.587 Drop inner 0.550 / 0.392 / 0.130 0.587 Drop outer 0.513 / 0.341 / 0.081 0.591
  • The second seed moves the scores by 0.001–0.006. Differences of that size are noise.
  • Drop inner gains most at IoU 0.75 (+0.014), where the fit of the box counts most.
  • Drop outer learns syllable fragments: on 3 s clips its median box is 0.19 s, against 0.24 s with nested boxes kept and 0.40 s for the median annotation of the unseen site. Its confidences also fall on the unseen site, so a threshold chosen on Hawai'i val does not carry over.

docs.title: Measured on Calls as a User Wants Them
docs.text:
The unseen site's labels do not box one unit: some species are boxed per song element, others per phrase. Box F1 then penalises element boxes on a phrase label as much as a miss, so it cannot tell whether finer boxes are better. To measure that, 260 five-second stretches of the unseen site (21.7 min) were relabelled by hand by one person: missed calls added, phrase boxes split where the elements stand alone, and kept together where they only make sense together (458 boxes before, 567 after). F1 at IoU 0.5 on these labels, with a 95% interval from a paired bootstrap over the stretches:

Comparison Best threshold and phrase gap Defaults (threshold 0.15, phrase gap 0.05 s) Drop outer vs drop inner −0.010 [−0.054, +0.031] −0.092 [−0.147, −0.035] Drop inner vs nested boxes kept +0.027 [−0.005, +0.059] +0.030 [−0.000, +0.059] Second seed vs nested boxes kept +0.001 [−0.023, +0.025]
  • Finer boxes are not what is wanted. Drop outer's element boxes, joined by the phrase gap, match the hand labels slightly worse than drop inner, and at the default threshold clearly worse.
  • Drop inner is ahead of keeping nested boxes in every measurement, on the unseen site and on the hand labels, but never beyond the noise (on the hand labels just at its edge).

The released model uses drop inner (make_nest.py inner). Like the looser rule, it is cheap and never scored below the labels without it.

docs.title: PCEN or Log-Floor Teachers
docs.text:
The released model sees log-floor spectrograms, and so do its teachers, so the whole chain uses one kind of spectrogram. The teachers of the earlier PCEN recipe saw PCEN spectrograms. To compare the two, the same rules (with the looser rule and drop inner) were also run with the PCEN teachers. Training split:

Dataset Clips used, PCEN teachers Clips used, log-floor teachers (released) Boxes, PCEN teachers Boxes, log-floor teachers Median round-2 box, PCEN / log-floor Northeastern US 106,405 109,255 199,531 200,231 0.42 s / 0.48 s Western US 27,450 28,796 41,193 46,053 0.56 s / 0.51 s Amazon Basin 13,266 14,949 27,756 33,346 0.82 s / 0.84 s Bird-Sounds-Global 69,864 70,766 123,049 129,815 0.38 s / 0.38 s All four 216,985 223,766 391,529 409,445

Boxes are counted after drop inner. The log-floor teachers find a qualifying call box in more clips, so 6,781 fewer clips are discarded (3% more bout-labelled training data, most of it in Northeastern US and Amazon Basin), and the median box length barely changes.

A student was trained on each set of labels, on log-floor images and with the hold-out recipe, twice with different seeds. Full recordings of the unseen site, window fusion as BirdBox runs it, phrase gap off:

Teachers Unseen site, IoU 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75, best threshold Unseen site, IoU 0.5 at the Hawai'i-val threshold Hand-labelled stretches, best F1 PCEN 0.549 / 0.392 / 0.128 0.389 0.462 PCEN, second seed 0.557 / 0.396 / 0.131 0.396 0.463 Log-floor (released recipe) 0.568 / 0.387 / 0.127 0.385 0.484 Log-floor, second seed 0.569 / 0.388 / 0.128 0.385 0.483

The differences below are log-floor minus PCEN teachers, first seed against first seed and second against second, at the Hawai'i-val threshold unless noted:

  • IoU 0.75 is a tie (−0.003 and −0.005, both within the noise), and IoU 0.25 is 0.012–0.019 higher with the log-floor teachers (best threshold).
  • IoU 0.5 is slightly lower: −0.004 [−0.016, +0.007] and −0.011 [−0.021, −0.002]. Against the October recipe (PCEN throughout), both seeds tie at IoU 0.5 (+0.002 and +0.003) and gain at IoU 0.75 (+0.009 and +0.007).
  • On the hand-labelled stretches both seeds score highest of all variants, +0.063 [+0.020, +0.107] over the October recipe.

The two log-floor seeds agree to within 0.001, while the two PCEN seeds differ by up to 0.008, so the IoU 0.5 gap is between 0.004 and 0.011. The log-floor teachers cost little, and in exchange no model in the chain depends on PCEN any more.

docs.title: Just-Bird Model Types and Format Parity
docs.text: BirdBox ships two pretrained models, Just-Bird and Birds-With-Labels. Both are released in multiple runtime formats to cover different deployment targets. This page covers the Just-Bird model. It documents every available format and shows how each one compares against the PyTorch baseline on identical recordings, so you can confirm that conversion or quantization does not degrade detection quality.

docs.title: Supported model formats
docs.text:
Each format targets a different deployment scenario. Install the matching runtime with python install.py --model-format <FORMAT>. See Installation for the full setup guide.

Format Typical use case Runtime .pt Default. PyTorch checkpoint, easiest to get started. PyTorch (CUDA or CPU) .onnx Cross-platform deployment, quantized variants available. ONNX Runtime (GPU or CPU) .tflite Edge devices and mobile targets. LiteRT / ai-edge-litert (CPU)

Each format needs an environment with its runtime

An environment runs .pt models and the format it was installed for. Loading a .onnx or .tflite model without its runtime stops with an error that names the install command. Create a separate environment for each format you use and run python install.py --model-format <FORMAT> in it. See Install Parameters for the full table.

docs.title: Verdict criteria
docs.text:
PASS

The model matches at least 90% of baseline detections, adds no more than 10% extra detections, and keeps the mean confidence difference at or below 0.05. The export is safe to use in place of the baseline.

WARN

One or more thresholds were exceeded. The model runs but performance may have degraded after conversion or quantization. Inspect the per-model detail below and compare detections on your own audio before deploying.

FAIL

The worker subprocess exited with an error. The model did not produce any detections. Check the per-model detail below for the full traceback.

docs.title: Metric glossary
docs.text:
Matching is one-to-one and recording by recording: a candidate detection can match a baseline detection of the same species when their 2D IoU (time and frequency) is at least 0.5. Pairs are taken in order of decreasing IoU, and each detection is used at most once.

Metric What it tells you Mean IoU Average time-and-frequency box overlap between matched pairs. 1.000 is a perfect overlap. Lower values mean boxes drifted in position or size. Mean Conf Δ Average absolute confidence difference on matched detections. Near 0.000 means the converted model is as confident as the baseline. Max Conf Δ Largest single confidence difference among matched detections. Surfaces worst-case outliers that the mean hides. Load (s) Wall-clock seconds to load the model file and build the detector. Detect (s) Wall-clock seconds spent running inference on all recordings. The times come from one machine and depend on whether a runtime uses the GPU, so they are not a speed benchmark.

docs.title: Species from BirdNET
docs.text:
Just-Bird draws a box around every bird vocalization but does not name the species. To name it, the boxes can be combined with BirdNET [13]: BirdNET V3.0 scores a 3 s window around a box, and the box takes the bird species with the highest score. The BirdNET website demo does this on its BirdBox tab.

This page compares where that window can sit, measured on annotated boxes with a known species. It is a study, not a BirdBox feature: BirdBox itself does not run BirdNET. The scripts are in scripts/birdnet_labels/.

docs.title: The Question
docs.text:
The website demo scores the windows BirdBox detects on, one every 1.5 s, alongside the detection. So a box usually has its species when it appears, and a box that grows, or changes with the sliders, needs no new scoring. The alternative is one window per box, centred on it, scored once the box can no longer change. Then the species appears later than the box: about 1.5 s after it when analysing a file, and about 4 s after the bird called when recording live.

The demo's windows are not centred on the box. Does that cost accuracy?

docs.title: Window Placements
docs.text:
Placement Windows for a box Used centred One 3 s window centred on the box. A box over 3 s: windows from its start, every 1.5 s. grid15 BirdBox's windows, one every 1.5 s. A box up to 1.5 s takes the window that owns its centre (the middle 1.5 s of a window, as in the window fusion). A longer box takes the windows from the one around its first 1.5 s to the one around its last. Demo grid075 As grid15, on windows every 0.75 s. Twice the BirdNET work. inside15 As grid15, and a box up to 1.5 s also takes a neighbouring window it lies wholly in. fit15 As grid15, but a box up to 3 s takes only the window that owns its centre when it lies wholly inside it. near15 As grid15, but a box up to 3 s always takes only the window that owns its centre.

With several windows, each species keeps its highest score. The window at the end of a recording is padded with silence, as BirdBox pads its last clip.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• Recordings: 116 recordings of four datasets, spread evenly over the file names:
    • Southern Sierra Nevada: 40 of 100 recordings of 10 min
    • Island of Hawai'i: 60 of 635 recordings of 5 min
    • Western United States: 4 of 33 recordings of 1 h
    • Northeastern United States: 12 of 285 recordings of 1 h
  • Boxes: the 11,552 annotated boxes of these recordings whose species is a bird of BirdNET V3.0. 1,216 further boxes were left out: 504 with an unidentified species (unknown, written ???? in the annotation files), and 712 of three species whose eBird code has no BirdNET V3.0 bird (amepip 401, pasfly 171, akepa1 140).
  • Model: BirdNET+ V3.0-preview3.1 Global 10K-pruned (FP16), the model of the BirdNET Live app and the website demo, run with ONNX Runtime 1.27 on the CPU.
  • Rules of the demo: only bird species count, and no location filter is applied. Top-1 means the highest-scoring bird is the annotated species, top-5 that it is among the five highest-scoring birds, which the demo's species menu lists when they score at least 0.05. The demo names a species only from a score of 0.35 on, otherwise the box stays unidentified ("Aves").

The annotated boxes stand in for the boxes BirdBox finds. Detected boxes differ from them, for example where calls are joined into phrases, so a demo run can score differently. Whether BirdNET V3.0 was trained on these recordings was not checked: that could make the absolute accuracies optimistic, but not change the comparison between placements, which all score the same recordings.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
All four datasets, 11,552 boxes. Differences in top-1 to centred with 95% intervals of a paired bootstrap over recordings:
