docs.title: Boxes of 1.5 to 3 s
docs.text:
This is the one place where BirdBox's windows lose: 0.025 in top-1 (95% interval −0.043 to −0.004). A centred window holds such a box whole, in its middle. On the grid, 1,313 of the 1,654 boxes lie wholly inside the window that owns their centre, and the rest take two windows.

Taking only the one window that holds the box (fit15), or always only the window that owns its centre (near15), recovers almost nothing. A window twice as dense (grid075) recovers about half, for twice the work:

Placement, boxes of 1.5 to 3 s Top-1 Minus centred (95% interval) Top-5 centred 0.613 0.834 grid15 0.588 −0.025 (−0.043 to −0.004) 0.838 fit15 0.591 −0.022 (−0.039 to −0.001) 0.839 near15 0.592 −0.021 (−0.036 to −0.003) 0.834 grid075 0.599 −0.014 (−0.026 to +0.001) 0.836

So even a grid window that holds the whole box names it less often than a window centred on it: what else the window holds matters. The right species is still among the five in the menu as often as with the centred window.

On the BirdNET website demo's sample soundscape, 4 of the 56 boxes BirdBox finds are 1.5 to 3 s long.

docs.title: How Good Is the Species at All?
docs.text:
The placement matters much less than how often BirdNET V3.0 names the annotated species at all: about half of the boxes in top-1, and three quarters in top-5. The Northeastern United States reaches 0.80, the other three datasets about 0.47.

A likely reason, not measured here: BirdNET V3.0 hears the whole 3 s window at all frequencies. Where several birds call at once, as in the dense choruses of Hawai'i and the Sierra Nevada, it may name the loudest one, not necessarily the one in the box.

docs.title: Ideas to Try
docs.text:
None of these are tested yet.

  • Centred window afterwards for boxes of 1.5 to 3 s: keep the fast species from the grid, then score a centred window and replace the species. That should recover the 0.025 for these boxes, but some boxes would switch species a moment after they appear.
  • Let BirdNET hear only the box: band-pass the window to the box's frequency band, or silence the window outside the box's time span, before BirdNET scores it.
  • Location and date: the demo's geomodel filter was off here. It removes species that do not occur at the place and time.
  • Combine windows differently: the mean instead of the highest score, or windows weighted by how much of the box they hold.
  • Detected instead of annotated boxes: run Just-Bird, match its boxes to the annotations, and score the species of the matched boxes, as a user of the demo would see them.
  • Which species are confused: a confusion table per dataset would show whether the errors are neighbours in the chorus or similar-sounding species.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
The BirdNET V3.0 files come from birdnet-live-app (assets/models): the FP16 model, its labels CSV and taxonomy.csv, which gives the eBird codes. Each dataset folder holds annotations.csv and soundscape_data_wav/ with the recordings at 32 kHz. Needs numpy, soundfile and onnxruntime.

M=BirdNET+_V3.0-preview3.1_Global_10K-pruned_FP16.onnx
L=BirdNET+_V3.0-preview3.1_Global_10K-pruned_Labels.csv
python scripts/birdnet_labels/label_windows.py $M $L taxonomy.csv Southern-Sierra-Nevada ssn.json --files=40
python scripts/birdnet_labels/label_windows.py $M $L taxonomy.csv Hawaii hawaii.json --files=60
python scripts/birdnet_labels/label_windows.py $M $L taxonomy.csv Western-US western.json --files=4
python scripts/birdnet_labels/label_windows.py $M $L taxonomy.csv Northeastern-US northeast.json --files=12
python scripts/birdnet_labels/summarize.py ssn.json hawaii.json western.json northeast.json

The four runs take about 30 minutes side by side on 20 CPU cores.

docs.title: Just-Bird Training
docs.text: How the Just-Bird model was trained: the recipe and why each step is there, the training curves of the released model, and the boxes per split. Just-Bird Label Refinement explains how the training labels were made.

docs.title: Training Recipe
docs.text:
The recipe was worked out on the Southern Sierra Nevada hold-out. Every model in this section was trained without Southern Sierra Nevada and tested on its full recordings, as in Performance on an Unseen Site. The released model repeats the last step with Southern Sierra Nevada added.

flowchart TD
  coco["YOLO11s<br/>COCO weights"]
  hawaii["Human labels, per call<br/>Hawai'i"]
  bouts["Human labels, per song<br/>Northeastern US,<br/>Western US, Amazon Basin,<br/>Bird-Sounds-Global"]
  t1["Teacher 1<br/>trained on Hawai'i only"]
  r1["Round-1 call labels"]
  t2["Teacher 2<br/>the call teacher of<br/>Birds-With-Labels"]
  r2["Round-2 call labels<br/>looser rule for<br/>call-sized boxes,<br/>nested boxes dropped"]
  ssn["Human labels, per call<br/>Southern Sierra Nevada"]
  final["Just-Bird<br/>10 epochs"]
  coco --> t1
  hawaii --> t1
  t1 -- "where" --> r1
  bouts --> r1
  r1 --> t2
  hawaii --> t2
  coco --> t2
  t2 -- "where" --> r2
  bouts --> r2
  r2 --> final
  hawaii --> final
  ssn --> final
  coco --> final

The arrows have the same meaning as in Birds-With-Labels Training. A teacher says where the calls are, inside the labels people drew per song. The next model learns from the call labels made this way. The teacher's scores are not distilled into the next model, so there are no dotted arrows. Each of the three models starts from the COCO weights.

On the Just-Bird pages, labels per song are called bout labels.

docs.title: Splitting Bouts into Calls
docs.text:
Trained on the human labels of all datasets, the model learns the bout style and draws boxes of several seconds on a new site. It then scores lower there than a model trained on Hawai'i alone (see the first two bars below). The bout labels are therefore replaced by call labels before the final training. A teacher model looks for calls inside each human box, and the call boxes it finds replace the box:

  • Round 1 uses a teacher trained on Hawai'i only, which never saw a bout box.
  • Round 2 uses a teacher trained on Hawai'i and the round-1 labels of the four bout-labelled datasets. It replaces the original human boxes again.
  • There is no round 3. Round 2 already tied round 1 on the unseen site (Why There Is No Third Round).

This is self-training: a teacher model labels the data and a student model is trained on these labels, also called pseudo-labels [16]. Training one model on the outputs of another is best known from knowledge distillation [10], where the two are now commonly called teacher and student. Making the student of one round the teacher of the next follows Noisy Student training, where each new student learns from the labels of the previous one and ends up better than its teacher [35]. Students with the same architecture as their teacher can likewise outperform it [5]. Unlike these methods, the teacher here does not label free data: it only places call boxes inside the boxes a human drew.

Round 2 often draws a phrase box and the syllable boxes inside it. The nested boxes are dropped before training (Nested Boxes).

Just-Bird Label Refinement explains the rule, what each round changes, and which boxes and clips are discarded.

docs.title: Each Step on the Unseen Site
docs.text:
• More data needs better labels. Adding the bout-labelled datasets with their human labels lowers F1 from 0.280 to 0.124. With the teacher's call labels, the same data raises it to 0.381–0.385.
  • Round 2 ties round 1 on full recordings (0.383 against 0.381). The round-1 model was trained on only a quarter of the data, so this is not a like-for-like comparison. Round 2 is kept because it discards less data and scores higher on 3 s clips (F1 0.368 against 0.343 at IoU 0.5, both trained on a quarter of the data). Its threshold also transfers: the one chosen on Hawai'i val loses almost nothing on the new site (0.383 against the best 0.384). Round 1 loses more (0.381 against 0.393).
  • The current recipe adds the looser rule and drops nested boxes from the round-2 labels. It trains the teachers and the model on log-floor spectrograms. At IoU 0.5 it ties the October recipe (0.385 against 0.383). At IoU 0.75 it gains (0.127 against 0.116 at the best threshold, see Performance on an Unseen Site).
  • The March 2026 recipe trained on the human labels for up to 100 epochs, with early stopping and augmentation from a hyperparameter search.

All bars use window fusion as BirdBox runs it, with the phrase gap off, and the threshold chosen on Hawai'i val.

docs.title: Ten Epochs
docs.text: This test used the PCEN version of the recipe (October 2026). Training longer does not help a new site. In a 30-epoch run, F1 on the unseen site is 0.361 after the first epoch and stays at 0.373–0.378 from epoch 6 on, while Hawai'i val holds at 0.588–0.591 from epoch 11 on. The checkpoints before epoch 30 are taken before that run's learning rate has decayed. The 10-epoch run decays fully within its 10 epochs and scores best on the unseen site (0.384, best threshold). Early stopping on Hawai'i val cannot see this, so the recipe uses a fixed 10 epochs. When the test data comes from other domains, how the model is selected matters, and validation data from the training domains is only a stand-in for the test domain [6].

docs.title: Training Curves of the Rounds
docs.text: Teacher 1 was trained for up to 100 epochs with early stopping (patience 20). Training stopped after epoch 50 and kept epoch 30 (mAP50 0.675). Teacher 2 and the final recipe run a fixed schedule that decays fully and keep the last epoch. On Hawai'i val the three end within about 0.05 mAP50 of each other (0.63–0.67). Only the unseen site separates them.

docs.title: Training Results
docs.text:
The figure shows the validation mAP and the box loss after each epoch. The validation set is the Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada val splits, the two datasets with call-level labels. The drop in training loss at epoch 8 is where mixup augmentation is switched off. The learning rate decays linearly to 3% of its start value at epoch 10 (see the recipe).

Model Checkpoint

The checkpoint with the best validation fitness was kept. Fitness is the mAP50-95 on the validation set. The best was the last epoch (10).

docs.title: Data Splits
docs.text:
Each dataset was split once into train, val and test, about 70/15/15 (see Dataset Splits). Just-Bird does not use these splits as they are. It has no test split and only a small validation set:

  • No test split. A test split from the same recordings only measures in-domain performance. Just-Bird was measured on a site it never saw instead (see Performance on an Unseen Site), so the test splits of all datasets are used for training.
  • Validation on call labels only. Only the val splits of Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada, the two datasets labelled per call, are used for validation. Bout-labelled val splits would reward loose boxes. Validation follows the training and picks the checkpoint, which was the last epoch (see Training Results). With over 600,000 training boxes, 2.6% for validation is still 16,755 boxes in 9,702 images.
  • Three val splits are left out. The val splits of Northeastern US, Western US and Amazon Basin are used neither for training nor for validation. The Western US one served as unseen data to check the phrase gap and the confidence threshold of the released model.
  • Bird-Sounds-Global is used in full for training, all three of its splits.

Boxes per dataset, counted per 3 s training image. Consecutive images overlap by 50%, so most calls are counted twice. For the four refined datasets these are the call boxes after label refinement, without the discarded clips.

docs.title: Just-Bird Model
docs.text:
The Just-Bird model has a single class, bird. It finds bird vocalizations of any species and draws a tight box around each call. Detections are merged with window fusion by default, which also joins same-band boxes less than 0.05 s apart into one phrase box (--phrase-gap, 0 keeps one box per call).

The model was trained on 1 November 2026. It sees log-floor spectrograms, and so do the teacher models that made its training labels.

Rolling noise floor (November 2026)

The model was trained on spectrograms whose noise floor was taken over each 60 s segment. BirdBox now takes it over the 60 s up to each clip's end (rolling floor), so boxes are final as soon as the audio reaches them. The weights are the same, and the two floors score level. Change in F1 at IoU 0.5 from the segment floor to the rolling floor, at thresholds 0.13 and 0.15:

  • Released model, Hawai'i validation recordings: −0.001 and −0.003 (both 95% intervals include zero).
  • Recipe trained without Southern Sierra Nevada, Hawai'i validation recordings: −0.002 and +0.000.
  • The same recipe, the unseen 10-minute Southern Sierra Nevada recordings: +0.003 and +0.005.

The scores below were measured with the segment floor.

More on Just-Bird:

  • Training: the training recipe and why each step is there, training curves and boxes per split.
  • Label Refinement: how the bout labels of four datasets were split into call labels.
  • Model Types: the export formats and how closely they match the PyTorch model.
  • Species from BirdNET: naming the species of the boxes with BirdNET V3.0, and where its window should sit.

docs.title: Training Data
docs.text:
The model was trained on six datasets:

  • Southwestern Amazon Basin
  • Island of Hawai'i
  • Northeastern United States
  • Southern Sierra Nevada mountain range
  • Western United States
  • Bird-Sounds-Global: annotated soundscapes from xeno-canto (Lifeplan and SystemShift projects) from many countries

Labels. Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada are annotated per call. The other datasets mostly put one box around a whole song or bout. Their boxes were replaced by single-call boxes in two rounds of self-training: a model trained on call-level labels found the calls inside each human box. A clip with a human box it could not replace was discarded, together with all its other boxes. Two further rules refine the labels. A call-sized human box is kept when a teacher box covers at least half of it (looser rule). Of two nested boxes, only the larger one is kept (nested boxes). Both teachers were trained on log-floor spectrograms, like the model itself. Training shows why, and Just-Bird Label Refinement how.

Recipe. YOLO11s, started from the COCO weights [18], trained for 10 epochs on log-floor spectrograms. The learning rate starts at 0.001 and decays linearly to 3% of it (0.00003) at epoch 10, after a 3-epoch warm-up. Mixup augmentation [36] (strength 0.3) is switched off for the last 3 epochs. Mosaic augmentation is not used. There is no early stopping.

docs.title: Performance on an Unseen Site
docs.text:
Because the model was trained on every dataset, none of them is left to test it on recordings from a site it has not seen. The transfer was therefore measured with the same recipe trained without Southern Sierra Nevada and then run on the full Southern Sierra Nevada recordings. This is a test on a domain the model never saw, like the camera-trap test of the WILDS benchmark, where models are evaluated on camera locations that are not in their training data [14]. For comparison, the recipes of the two earlier Just-Bird models (October and March 2026) were retrained and tested in the same way.

The score is F1 over boxes on full recordings: a box counts as found when it overlaps a label by at least the given IoU, each label matched once. Boxes are merged with window fusion as BirdBox runs it (nested boxes dropped, phrase gap off). The first three columns use the threshold that is best on these recordings, separately for each column. A user cannot know that threshold in advance, so it is a best case. The last column uses the threshold chosen on Hawai'i val, as a user would.

Recipe IoU 0.25, best threshold IoU 0.5, best threshold IoU 0.75, best threshold IoU 0.5, threshold chosen on Hawai'i val Current (November 2026) 0.568 0.387 0.127 0.385 October 2026 0.541 0.384 0.116 0.383 March 2026 0.465 0.281 0.059 0.250

Against the October recipe, the current one gains where the fit of a box counts. With each recipe at its Hawai'i-val threshold, it gains +0.009 at IoU 0.75 (95% interval +0.000 to +0.016, paired bootstrap over the 100 recordings) and +0.027 at IoU 0.25. At IoU 0.5 the two tie. A second training run with another seed scores within 0.001 of these numbers.

The gain at IoU 0.75 comes from the new labels, not from the spectrogram. Log-floor with the October labels does not gain (−0.003). The new labels on PCEN with gain 1 gain as much (+0.009). PCEN with gain 1 is a variant of PCEN that, like log-floor, removes the recording level from the image completely.

The graph shows precision, recall and F1 at IoU 0.5 for every confidence threshold. The curves come from the model trained without Southern Sierra Nevada, not from the released weights, which were trained on it. The dashed and dotted lines are the October and March recipes, retrained the same way, not the released models.

At IoU 0.75 a box has to fit the call closely. Here the current recipe is ahead of the October one at almost every threshold:

  • Confidence threshold: 0.15, the default in detect_birds.py and the Demo. It was the best threshold of the October model and was kept. For the current recipe, the best threshold on the Hawai'i validation recordings is 0.13 to 0.14. It carries over to the unseen site with little loss (0.385 against the best 0.387). At 0.15 the recipe scores 0.382 there, 0.003 less than at 0.13.

  • Phrase gap: some Southern Sierra Nevada labels box a whole phrase where the model boxes single syllables. This lowers the scores at IoU 0.5 and above. The default phrase gap of 0.05 s adds little, F1 at IoU 0.5 at the best threshold:

    • Unseen site, recipe trained without Southern Sierra Nevada: 0.387 without the gap, 0.391 with it (October recipe: 0.384 and 0.389).
    • Song-labelled Western-US validation minutes, released model: 0.230 with and without it (October model: 0.171 and 0.172).
    • Call-level labels (Hawai'i val): it costs 0.005 (0.579 and 0.574).

    If your annotations box single calls, pass --phrase-gap 0.

  • Western-US validation: on these song-labelled minutes, which no model trained on, the released model reaches 0.230 at IoU 0.5 with the phrase gap off, against 0.171 for the October model (each at its best threshold; 0.209 against 0.168 at the defaults). Phrase Gap shows the other gaps.

  • In-domain: on the full Hawai'i validation recordings, the released model reaches F1 0.570 at IoU 0.5 (threshold 0.14, phrase gap off), against 0.593 for the October model. At IoU 0.75, each at its best threshold, the two tie (0.284 against 0.285). The loss is the price of a spectrogram that does not change with the recording level. PCEN kept part of the level in the image. The October model apparently used it to tell the faint background calls of the Hawai'i recordings, which the annotators mostly left unlabelled, from the louder labelled ones. When the Hawai'i recordings are played 12 dB quieter, a PCEN model makes many more faint false alarms. Most of the extra false alarms are faint sounds 10–20 dB above the noise floor, many of them visible calls without a label. A model trained on PCEN images with gain 1, which also removes the level, loses the same way. So the loss is not specific to log-floor.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This chapter describes the available models, gives insight into the underlying dataset splits and demonstrates their performance based on individual evaluation and testsets with various metrics.

BirdBox accepts YOLO models in multiple formats such as .pt, .onnx and .tflite. Trained models for this task can be found on the TUC-Cloud. Alternatively, you can train your own model on a custom dataset by using the code available in the BirdBox-Train repository.

Restricted Access

BirdBox-Train is currently only accessible to members of the BirdNET-Team.

To run benchmarks with a model of your choice and a custom dataset see CLI Reference.

Recommended model

Just-Bird is the recommended model and the default in the Demo and the pipeline scripts. It detects bird vocalizations with a single bird class. For species-level detection, use the Birds-With-Labels model. It finds calls as Just-Bird does and names their species where it can.

docs.title: Available Models and Respective Datasets
docs.text:
The available models are trained with datasets from Zenodo.org. The utilized datasets are:

  • Southwestern Amazon Basin
  • Island of Hawai'i
  • Northeastern United States
  • Southern Sierra Nevada mountain range
  • Western United States

BirdBox provides two models, both trained on all five datasets and on Bird-Sounds-Global, annotated soundscapes from xeno-canto:

  • Just-Bird (recommended), a single bird class
  • Birds-With-Labels, 634 classes: the 281 species of the five datasets, 351 further species from Bird-Sounds-Global, the class unknown and bird for calls of any species

docs.title: Dataset Splits
docs.text:
Each dataset is split once into a training, a validation and a test split. The split aims at 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test data for every species. The counted quantity is the number of labels within a split, not the number of files. For example, a file with five aldfly annotations is counted as five, not one.

The two models use these splits differently:

Birds-With-Labels Just-Bird Training train splits (Bird-Sounds-Global included) train and test splits of all datasets, and the val split of Bird-Sounds-Global Validation val splits val splits of Hawai'i and Southern Sierra Nevada only (labelled per call) Test test splits none: tested on a site it never saw, with a model trained without that site Train/val/test share of the boxes 69.5/14.9/15.5 98.6/1.4/0

Birds-With-Labels is a species model and is tested in-domain on the test splits, so it keeps the 70/15/15 split. Bird-Sounds-Global has its own split, by recording rather than by species. Just-Bird is measured on an unseen site instead, so the test splits are more useful as training data. It validates on call labels only, and with over a million training boxes a small validation set is enough. See Just-Bird Data Splits and Birds-With-Labels Species Distribution for the counts.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
There exist multiple reasons why the 70/15/15 split of each dataset is not trivial:

  1. it is strictly forbidden to split overlapping data into different data-splits (but 50% overlap by default)
  2. temporally adjacent recordings may record the same bird with the same background noise twice [28]
  3. single three-second clips often contain multiple annotations from different species

The first and second problem can be solved by dividing the soundscape recordings into one-minute chunks before any data is split. Three-second clips with overlap are then only generated within these one-minute files. The resulting three-second clips can then only be sorted into the same dataset split. Therefore, no direct overlap between splits is possible and the problem of temporal data leakage is mitigated.

However, combined with the third problem, this limits the capabilities of the dataset-splitter. From now on, only one minute chunks can be sorted into a distinct split.

docs.title: Rare Species
docs.text:
Yet some rare species only occur in one or two minutes of the original audio. This makes it impossible to split them into three datasets.

One could think about rather complex data augmentation techniques like cutting out the rare vocalizations and inserting them into multiple different background noises. This newly generated synthetic data could then be split. But this data scaling can still be employed after a first successful deployment of BirdBox.

Since this project is in its early stages, it has been decided to just consider every species with less than 100 annotations as rare. For Birds-With-Labels, those rare species are only used for training. The metrics during training and hyperparameter tuning (evaluation dataset) and for testing (test dataset) are computed only with splittable, often occurring species. The splits that Just-Bird uses were made later and fold rare species into the class unknown before splitting, so their boxes are split like all others. For Just-Bird every box is a bird anyway.

docs.title: Clipping
docs.text: Within each dataset, the amount of labels of a species has been reduced if it exceeded 10,000. This applies to both models. Bird-Sounds-Global was not clipped. However, this limit is soft because we can only discard or keep entire three second clips. If a spectrogram contains a species which should be clipped, but also a rare one, the entire spectrogram is kept. Thus adding another annotation above 10,000.

docs.title: Increase of Annotation Amount
docs.text:
Additionally, the amount of annotations in the dataset exceed the amount of original annotations by far due to two reasons:

  • 50% overlap leads to label duplicates within the same dataset-split
  • 3 second clips cut long annotations (e.g. 3 minutes) into multiple small ones

This behavior is intended. See How it works.

docs.title: ID to Species Mapping Compatibility
docs.text:
Because BirdBox is capable of running different models for the detection, it has to manage multiple different id to species mappings. The possible mappings are defined in SPECIES_MAPPING in src/config.py. Those mappings directly refer to the utilized conf.yaml during the training of the corresponding YOLO-model.

The class-id decoding depends on the selected mapping. This mapping is set like this:

  • CLI: pass explicit --species-mapping (details)
  • onnx_export.py without --species-mapping: mapping is inferred from the model file name (get_species_mapping_for_model() in src/config.py)

Mapping/Model Mismatch

If the species mapping does not match the selected model, the species labels in the output will be silently invalid. Always pass the --species-mapping value that corresponds to the model you are running.
